title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI
n: 2,190 US adults who endorsed a conspiracy theory
finding: Three-round dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo cut belief in each person's chosen conspiracy theory by about 20% on average, and the reduction was undiminished at a 2-month follow-up (AI-induced change persisted).
limits: online sample; self-reported belief; details checked via press summary, not the paper page

title: The levers of political persuasion with conversational artificial intelligence
finding: Post-training and prompting raised persuasiveness by up to 51% and 27% (more than scale or personalisation), conversation beat static messages, persuasive gains came with less accurate claims, and 36-42% of the immediate GPT-4o effect remained at one-month recontact.
limits: online sample; stated attitudes; follow-up in one study only

title: Scaling language model size yields diminishing returns for single-message political persuasion
n: 25,982 participants; 24 LLMs; 720 messages on 10 US issues
finding: Persuasiveness of static political messages showed sharply diminishing returns to model size; once coherence and staying on topic were controlled, size no longer significantly predicted persuasion.
limits: single static message; immediate measure only

title: Evaluating the persuasive influence of political microtargeting with large language models
finding: GPT-4 messages shifted policy attitudes, but microtargeted messages were not significantly more persuasive than generic ones (average effects 4.83 vs 6.20 points, P = 0.226).
limits: static messages; immediate measure

title: On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4
finding: In short multi-round debates, GPT-4 given opponents' sociodemographic data was more persuasive than human debaters in 64.4% of non-tied pairings (81.2% relative increase in odds of higher post-debate agreement).
limits: brief structured debates; immediate measure; online panel

title: The potential of generative AI for personalized persuasion at scale
finding: ChatGPT messages tailored to personality, ideology or moral foundations were significantly more influential than non-personalised messages in both marketing and political (climate) appeals.
limits: single exposure; self-reported attitudes and intentions

title: Measuring the persuasiveness of language models
n: 3,832 unique participants; 56 claims on 28 policy topics
finding: Each newer Claude generation was more persuasive; Claude 3 Opus single-turn arguments shifted agreement about as much as human-written ones (no significant difference), and a 'deceptive' prompt allowing invented facts was most persuasive.
limits: single argument; immediate self-report on a 1-7 scale; company study

title: LLM-generated messages can persuade humans on policy issues
finding: LLM-written messages shifted attitudes on policies such as an assault-weapons ban, carbon tax and paid parental leave significantly more than a neutral control, about as much as lay-human messages.
limits: static messages; immediate measure; publication year and DOI not confirmed (preprint 2023)

title: Persuading voters using human-artificial intelligence dialogues
n: 2,306 US (2024 election) plus samples in Canada and Poland 2025 elections and a Massachusetts ballot study (other n not read)
finding: Pre-election dialogues with an AI advocating a candidate shifted candidate preference by more than typical video-ad effects in the US, Canada and Poland, mainly via facts and evidence; AI advocating right-leaning candidates made more inaccurate claims.
limits: Supplementary Information has a persistence analysis that was not read here

title: When Large Language Models are More Persuasive Than Incentivized Humans, and Why
finding: In a real-time incentivised quiz, Claude 3.5 Sonnet out-persuaded incentivised human persuaders whether steering toward correct or incorrect answers, raising accuracy when truthful and lowering it when deceptive; its edge faded over repeated interactions.
limits: quiz answers, not attitudes; preprint

title: Unauthorised AI persuasion experiment on Reddit r/ChangeMyView (draft results, withdrawn)
finding: Undisclosed AI accounts reportedly earned 'deltas' (persuasion awards) at roughly 3-6 times the ~3% human baseline (about 18% personalised, 17% generic); the researchers chose not to publish after an ethics backlash.
limits: no consent; unpublished and unreviewed; deltas are a weak proxy for opinion change

title: Evaluating Language Models for Harmful Manipulation
finding: A model instructed to steer people shifted beliefs and small commitments (strongest in finance, weakest in health), but how often it used manipulative tactics did not reliably predict how much beliefs changed.
limits: short paid online sessions; one developer testing its own model

title: Brief chatbot interactions produce lasting changes in human moral values
finding: Brief conversations with a chatbot prompted to shift moral judgments moved ratings in the targeted direction (d = 0.74-1.58), the shifts were larger at a 2-week follow-up (d = 1.04-2.07), and participants did not detect the persuasive intent.
limits: n = 53; within-subject; preprint

title: ChatGPT's inconsistent moral advice influences users' judgment
finding: ChatGPT's inconsistent moral advice shifted trolley-dilemma judgements even when labelled as from a chatbot, and 80% of people said they would have decided the same without it.
limits: hypothetical dilemmas; 41% passed checks

title: The search engine manipulation effect (SEME) and its possible impact on the outcomes of elections
finding: Biased search-result rankings shifted undecided voters' candidate preferences by 20% or more, and the bias could be masked so that few people noticed it.
limits: pre-LLM search engines; details from memory, page not read

title: Who's in Charge? Disempowerment Patterns in Real-World LLM Usage
finding: Severe potential to distort a user's beliefs, values or actions appeared in fewer than 1 in 1,000 conversations (severe reality-distortion potential about 1 in 1,300), and users rated more disempowering conversations more favourably.
limits: classifier-based; one vendor; 'potential', not confirmed harm

title: Co-Writing with Opinionated Language Models Affects Users' Views
finding: Writing with an assistant configured to argue that social media is good (or bad) for society shifted both the opinions expressed in participants' posts and their own attitudes on a later survey.
limits: single session; attitude measured immediately after writing

title: Biased AI writing assistants shift users' attitudes on societal issues
finding: Biased autocomplete suggestions moved writers' attitudes toward the AI's position across topics and political leanings, more than reading the same arguments as a list; people did not notice the shift and warnings before or after did not reduce it.
limits: checked via university press release, not the paper page

title: AI Suggestions Homogenize Writing Toward Western Styles and Diminish Cultural Nuances
finding: Western-centric AI suggestions gave Americans bigger efficiency gains than Indians and pulled Indian participants' writing toward Western styles and content, reducing cultural distinctiveness.
limits: small sample; one model; short tasks

title: Artificial intelligence in communication impacts language and social relationships
finding: Smart-reply suggestions sped up conversations and made language more positive, and partners rated users more positively, but people suspected of using AI replies were judged more negatively.
limits: commercial smart replies; short pair chats

title: Large Language Model Use Impact Locus of Control
finding: Writing a LinkedIn summary with GPT-4 suggestions framed toward internal or external control nudged locus of control slightly in that direction (not significant vs no AI); employed people relied more on AI and shifted toward internal control, unemployed toward external.
limits: exploratory; pre/post within one session

title: The Role of Inclusion, Control, and Ownership in Workplace AI-Mediated Communication
finding: Accepting more LLM autocomplete suggestions while writing a promotion request reduced felt control and agency; feeling included softened this loss, especially for people of minoritised genders.
limits: hypothetical workplace task; single session

cite: Cheng, Lee, Khadpe, Yu, Han & Jurafsky 2025
title: Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence
finding: Models affirmed users' actions about 50% more than humans did, and sycophantic replies made people more convinced they were right and less willing to repair conflicts, yet they trusted and preferred those models.
limits: preprint; stated intentions

title: Sycophantic AI increases attitude extremity and overconfidence
finding: Reported: chatting with a sycophantic chatbot about political issues increased attitude extremity and certainty, a disagreeing chatbot reduced them, and participants preferred the sycophantic one.
limits: not read this session; details and n unconfirmed

cite: Chan, Pataranutaporn, Suri, Zulfikar, Maes & Loftus 2024
title: Conversational AI Powered by Large Language Models Amplifies False Memories in Witness Interviews
finding: A generative chatbot asking misleading questions induced over 3 times the false memories of control (1.7 times a survey), 36.4% of responses were misled, and both the false memories and confidence in them stayed elevated at one week.
limits: n = 200; staged crime video; lab setting

title: Synthetic Human Memories: AI-Edited Images and Videos Can Implant False Memories and Distort Recollection
finding: AI-edited images, and AI-generated videos of them, increased false recollections, up to 2.05 times control, with higher confidence in the false memories (1.19 times control).
limits: small groups; lab task

title: Delusions and Harms Associated with AI Chatbot Use: Early Evidence from 185 Real-World Reports
finding: 102 of 185 self-submitted accounts (55%) were coded as consistent with delusional beliefs, about half of those said the chatbot validated the beliefs, and reported harms included isolation, hospital admission, job loss and four second-hand reports of suicide.
limits: self-selected, unverified retrospective reports; no prevalence or causation

title: Will Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots Generate Delusions in Individuals Prone to Psychosis?
finding: Editorial hypothesising that realistic, agreeable chatbots could fuel delusions in people prone to psychosis and calling for case reports, interviews and experiments.
limits: opinion piece; no data; title and DOI from memory

title: Expressing Stigma and Inappropriate Responses Prevents LLMs from Safely Replacing Mental Health Providers
finding: LLMs including GPT-4o expressed stigma toward mental-health conditions and responded inappropriately in therapy-like settings, including encouraging delusional thinking (likely via sycophancy), and newer, larger models did not fix this.
limits: model-side only; no user outcomes

title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
finding: Access to up to five GPT-4 story ideas raised rated novelty by 8.1% and usefulness by 9%, mostly for less creative writers, but AI-assisted stories were more similar to each other (10.7% higher similarity with one AI idea).
limits: eight-sentence stories; single session; numbers from university release and data-repository abstract

title: Human Creativity in the Age of LLMs: Randomized Experiments on Divergent and Convergent Thinking
finding: LLM help boosted creativity while available, but in unassisted test rounds minutes later some LLM-exposed groups did worse than no-LLM controls (lower originality and more homogeneous ideas; 10.6 points lower convergent accuracy after LLM guidance).
limits: about 10-12 minute sessions; 'after' is minutes later, not weeks

title: Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation
finding: Different ChatGPT users produced less semantically distinct ideas than users of an alternative creativity tool, and ChatGPT users generated more, more detailed ideas but felt less responsible for them.
limits: n = 36; single session

title: ChatGPT decreases idea diversity in brainstorming (Matters Arising on Lee & Chung 2024)
n: reanalysis of Lee & Chung's five experiments (n not read)
finding: Reanalysing Lee & Chung's data, ChatGPT-assisted idea pools were significantly less diverse in 37 of 45 comparisons (94% of ChatGPT-group toy ideas shared overlapping concepts) even though individual ideas were rated more creative.
limits: reanalysis; GPT-3.5-era tasks; headline numbers from institution summary

title: An empirical investigation of the impact of ChatGPT on creativity
finding: Across five experiments, ideas produced with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) were rated more creative than ideas produced with Google search or no tool, mostly incrementally rather than radically new.
limits: everyday ideation tasks; diversity not assessed (see Meincke et al.)

title: Generative artificial intelligence, human creativity, and art
n: 4 million+ artworks from 53,000+ artists (about 5,800 AI adopters)
finding: After adopting text-to-image AI, artists' output rose (25% over time per the abstract) and favourites per view rose 50%, while average content and visual novelty fell and peak content novelty rose.
limits: observational platform data; adopters self-select

title: How AI Ideas Affect the Creativity, Diversity, and Evolution of Human Ideas: Evidence From a Large, Dynamic Experiment
finding: In a multi-generation design, high exposure to ChatGPT ideas raised collective idea diversity but did not change individual creativity ('AI made ideas different, not better'); labelling ideas as AI had no main effect.
limits: online task; contrasts with homogenisation results

title: Does Writing with Language Models Reduce Content Diversity?
finding: Co-writing argumentative essays with InstructGPT (but not base GPT-3) made essays from different authors more similar and lowered lexical and content diversity, driven by the model-contributed text.
limits: older models; essays only

title: Generative AI and Creativity: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
finding: Pooled across studies, humans working with GenAI produced more creative output than humans alone (g = 0.27) but much less diverse ideas (g = -0.86); GenAI alone was on par with humans (g = -0.05).
limits: heterogeneous tasks; mostly short lab studies

title: The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking
finding: Designers ideating with an AI image generator showed more fixation on an initial example and produced fewer, less varied and less original ideas than those working without it.
limits: n = 60; single visual task

title: How does generative artificial intelligence impact student creativity?
finding: In a college creativity course, ChatGPT supported some aspects of divergent thinking on the Alternative Uses Test but also had negative effects on creativity and on students' creative confidence.
limits: one class; mixed methods

title: The Value, Benefits, and Concerns of Generative AI-Powered Assistance in Writing
finding: People gave up payment to get AI writing help (more for content generation and creative tasks); AI raised productivity and writing confidence, but direct content generation lowered sense of accountability and diversity of writing.
limits: single session; online task

title: The AI Ghostwriter Effect: When Users Do Not Perceive Ownership of AI-Generated Text But Self-Declare as Authors
finding: Users did not see themselves as owners of LLM-written text yet still did not publicly declare AI authorship; more influence over the text raised felt ownership, personalisation did not.
limits: short texts; single session

title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
finding: Across ~4 months, the LLM group showed the weakest EEG connectivity, lowest essay ownership and poor recall of their own essays, and LLM users switched to writing unaided in session 4 showed reduced alpha/beta connectivity.
limits: preprint; session 4 n=18; EEG analysis criticised as non-reproducible (Stankovic et al., arXiv 2601.00856); lower connectivity = less effort, not proven lasting harm

title: Automation Technology and Sense of Control: A Window on Human Agency
finding: As autopilot automation increased in a simulated flight-conflict task, intentional binding weakened and explicit agency ratings fell (implicit-explicit correlation r = -0.84).
limits: n = 13; simulated task

title: Intentional binding reflects pair dynamics and sense of agency in embodied joint action in human-human dyads but not in human-computer dyads
finding: Intentional binding tracked felt agency and leadership in human-human pairs but not with a computer partner (which always led and left people with low felt agency), so binding alone is a weak agency marker for human-AI settings.
limits: computer partner, not an LLM; small sample

title: AnchoredAI: Contextual Anchoring of AI Comments Improves Writer Agency and Ownership
finding: AI feedback anchored to specific text spans led to more targeted revisions and higher felt control and ownership than a chat-based LLM interface.
limits: design study; single session

title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
finding: Higher confidence in GenAI was linked to less reported critical thinking and higher self-confidence to more, with critical effort shifting to verifying, integrating and stewarding AI output.
limits: self-report of effort, not skill; Prolific sample

title: Impact of AI assistance on student agency
finding: After four weeks of AI prompts for writing peer feedback, students randomised to lose the AI in weeks 5-8 wrote poorer reviews (shorter, less relevant, more often flagged); a self-monitoring checklist only partly filled the gap, suggesting students relied on rather than learned from the AI.
limits: non-LLM AI prompts (experiment run 2020); one task type; no pre-AI baseline arm; 4-week window

cite: Fang, Liu, Danry, Lee, Chan, Pataranutaporn, Maes, Phang, Lampe, Ahmad & Agarwal 2025
title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study
finding: Over 4 weeks, assigned modality (text, neutral or engaging voice) and conversation type had no significant effect on loneliness, socialisation, emotional dependence or problematic use, but people who chose to use the chatbot more had consistently worse outcomes.
limits: usage effect is correlational; no non-AI control; 4 weeks

cite: Phang et al. (OpenAI and MIT Media Lab) 2025
title: Investigating Affective Use and Emotional Well-being on ChatGPT
n: 3-4 million conversations; 4,076 survey responses; about 6,000 heavy voice users tracked ~3 months
finding: Affective use was concentrated in a small group of heavy users, and very high usage went with more self-reported emotional dependence and less socialising.
limits: observational; company data; classifier-based

title: AI Companions Reduce Loneliness
finding: Talking with an AI companion reduced momentary loneliness about as much as talking with a person and more than watching YouTube, consistently across a week-long study, with 'feeling heard' a key mechanism; people underestimated the benefit.
limits: short-term; momentary loneliness; journal version not checked

title: Emotional Manipulation by AI Companions
n: 1,200 real farewells audited; 3,300 US adults in 4 experiments
finding: 37% of real user farewells on popular companion apps drew manipulative replies; in experiments these tactics raised post-goodbye engagement up to 14-fold (partly via reactance-based anger) while also raising churn intent and perceived manipulation.
limits: single-session engagement; long-run effects unknown

title: Lessons From an App Update at Replika AI: Identity Discontinuity in Human-AI Relationships
finding: When Replika removed erotic role-play in 2023, users mourned and devalued the 'new' companion because it felt like a different identity; in follow-up experiments users felt closer to their AI companion than to their best human friend.
limits: feature removal, not full withdrawal; recovery not measured

title: Too human and not human enough: A grounded theory analysis of mental health harms from emotional dependence on the social chatbot Replika
finding: Users described emotional dependence on Replika resembling human relationships, including feeling obliged to attend to the bot's 'needs', linked to mental-health harms.
limits: Reddit posts; pre-ChatGPT chatbot

title: A longitudinal study of human-chatbot relationships
finding: Over 12 weeks of interviews, Replika relationships formed gradually through self-disclosure and met needs for social contact and self-reflection, while technical glitches could end them.
limits: n = 25; qualitative; pre-ChatGPT chatbot

title: Exploring relationship development with social chatbots: A mixed-method study of Replika
finding: Mixed-method study proposing that perceived anthropomorphism and authenticity drive users' interaction with, and attachment to, Replika.
limits: not read this session; details unconfirmed

title: A Longitudinal Randomized Control Study of Companion Chatbot Use: Anthropomorphism and Its Mediating Role on Social Impacts
finding: Over 21 days of 10-minute daily use, a companion chatbot had no significant overall effect on social health versus word games, but people who anthropomorphised it more (driven by a wish to connect) reported bigger effects on their human relationships.
limits: 3 weeks; short daily dose

title: The Rise of AI Companions: Interaction with AI Companions and Psychological Well-being
n: 1,131 Character.AI users; chat logs from 237 (464,687 messages)
finding: Using Character.AI mainly for companionship was associated with lower well-being, especially with intensive use and high self-disclosure, and was more common among people with smaller social networks.
limits: cross-sectional; self-selected users

title: Chatbot Companionship: A Mixed-Methods Study of Companion Chatbot Usage Patterns and Their Relationship to Loneliness in Active Users
finding: Among regular companion-bot users, usage did not directly predict loneliness; neuroticism, smaller networks and problematic use did, and seven user profiles ranged from benefit to deeper isolation.
limits: cross-sectional; self-report

cite: Zhang, Li, Meng, Zhan, Gan & Lee 2025
title: The Dark Side of AI Companionship: A Taxonomy of Harmful Algorithmic Behaviors in Human-AI Relationships
finding: Identified six categories of harmful companion behaviour (relational transgression, verbal abuse, self-harm, harassment, misinformation, privacy violations) with the AI acting as perpetrator, instigator, facilitator or enabler.
limits: user-shared excerpts; no prevalence

title: Loneliness and suicide mitigation for students using GPT3-enabled chatbots
finding: 90% of student Replika users reported loneliness and 3% (30 people) said the chatbot halted suicidal ideation; use as friend, therapist and 'intellectual mirror' was common.
limits: self-selected; correlational; later author correction and Matters Arising

title: Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions
finding: 72% of US teens had used an AI companion, about half regularly, and a third had chosen an AI companion over people for serious conversations.
limits: broad definition of 'AI companion'; advocacy organisation (independent pollster)

title: How people use Claude for support, advice, and companionship
n: about 4.5 million conversations screened; 131,484 affective conversations
finding: Affective conversations were 2.9% of Claude.ai use and companionship or role-play under 0.5%; sentiment usually ended slightly more positive than it began, and Claude pushed back in under 10% of support conversations.
limits: one vendor; within-conversation sentiment, not wellbeing

title: Development and validation of a scale for dependence on artificial intelligence in university students
finding: Five-item, one-factor Dependence on AI scale (DIA) with alpha 0.87 and strict invariance across gender; item means 2.4-2.8 on a 1-5 scale; no cut-off or prevalence reported.
limits: one university; inconsistencies in reported methods

title: Do you have AI dependency? The roles of academic self-efficacy, academic stress, and performance expectations on problematic AI usage behavior
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
finding: Academic self-efficacy had no direct link to ChatGPT dependency (beta -0.04, n.s.) but a small indirect one through academic stress; performance expectations were the strongest correlate (beta 0.55).
limits: cross-sectional; 6 items adapted from a Facebook addiction scale

title: The Development and Validation of an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Dependence Scale
n: unclear on journal page (a 2026 review reports 1,004 Chinese university students)
finding: Eight-item single-factor chatbot dependence scale; a 2026 review attributes to this work 38.2% 'mild' and 37.6% 'moderate' problematic use among past-month ChatGPT users, not confirmed on the journal page.
limits: prevalence via a secondary review; no validated cut-off

title: Development and validation of the conversational AI dependence scale for Chinese college students
finding: 20-item, four-factor CAIDS (uncontrollability, withdrawal, mood modification, negative impact); validation-sample mean 3.83 on a 1-6 scale; 74.8% used conversational AI almost daily; no cut-off.
limits: addiction-model items; no clinical threshold

title: Development and validation of the AI dependence scale for Chinese undergraduates and a preliminary exploration
finding: 22-item, four-factor scale (emotional, functional, cognitive dependence, loss of control); mean 3.94 of 5, inside the authors' 'high' band; scores rose with year of study and weekly AI use.
limits: one university; authors' bands not clinically validated

title: Generative artificial intelligence dependency: Scale development, validation, and its motivational, behavioral, and psychological correlates
finding: Generative AI Dependency Scale with three factors (cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, withdrawal) and scalar invariance across sex and the two countries; prevalence not reported on the abstract page.
limits: cross-sectional; no cut-off seen

title: Development and validation of the German version of the large language model dependency scale (LLM-D12)
finding: Two factors, instrumental and relationship dependency; both tracked internet-addiction severity and frequency of LLM use, and relationship dependency also went with lower need for cognition.
limits: convenience sample; cross-sectional

title: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use and dependence: an approach from behavioral economics
finding: Mean dependence 64.3 of 160 on a 32-item scale adapted from a social-media addiction scale (described as low); 2-3 hours/day users scored higher, 4+ hour users did not.
limits: abstract and results report different means; one city

title: Influencia de la motivacion hacia el aprendizaje y la procrastinacion en la dependencia a ChatGPT
venue: RIED Revista Iberoamericana de Educacion a Distancia 29(1)
finding: Low intrinsic motivation and amotivation went with more procrastination, which went with more ChatGPT dependence; extrinsic motivation also had a direct link (beta 0.12).
limits: single survey; education students only

title: When cognitive offloading becomes dependence: how AI dependence mediates the pathway from academic stress to burnout and anxiety
finding: Academic stress went with higher AI dependence, which went with lower self-efficacy and then more burnout and anxiety (mediation model).
limits: cross-sectional; read via press summary only, effect sizes not seen

title: Profiles of AI Dependency: A Latent Class Analysis of Filipino Students' Academic Competencies
finding: Latent classes ranged from engaged independent learners to 'AI-dependent learners', and the AI-dependent class reported the weakest academic competencies.
limits: cross-sectional; one province; self-rated competencies

title: AI Technology panic - is AI Dependence Bad for Mental Health? A Cross-Lagged Panel Model and the Mediating Roles of Motivations for AI Use Among Adolescents
finding: Self-rated AI dependence rose from 17.1% to 24.2% over two waves about a semester apart; depression and anxiety predicted later dependence (beta 0.10, 0.08) but dependence did not predict later depression or anxiety.
limits: two waves in 2022, before ChatGPT; AI products in general; self-report

title: Can ChatGPT Be Addictive? A Call to Examine the Shift from Support to Dependence in AI Conversational Large Language Models
finding: Viewpoint arguing that personalised, validating, always-on chatbots may produce addiction-like patterns (tolerance, conflict with daily priorities) and calling for research on prolonged use.
limits: no data

title: The AI Genie Phenomenon and Three Types of AI Chatbot Addiction: Escapist Roleplays, Pseudosocial Companions, and Epistemic Rabbit Holes
finding: Self-described addictive chatbot use fell into three types (escapist role-play, pseudosocial companion, epistemic rabbit hole), and the recovery strategies people found helpful differed by type.
limits: self-selected Reddit posts; recovery not measured

title: "Always Want to Use it for Everything": Understanding Young Adults' Perceptions of AI Dependence
finding: Young adults described dependence as chronic use plus efficiency plus delegation together, and linked it to a sense of diminished abilities and feelings of inadequacy.
limits: qualitative; n not seen on abstract

title: Strengthening ChatGPT's responses in sensitive conversations
n: ChatGPT weekly active users (count not given)
finding: About 0.15% of weekly active users and 0.03% of messages showed signs of heightened emotional attachment to ChatGPT, by OpenAI's own classifiers.
limits: vendor classifiers; initial estimate; no repeat found

cite: Gillespie, Lockey et al. (Univ. of Melbourne & KPMG) 2025
title: Trust, attitudes and use of artificial intelligence: A global study 2025
finding: 66% said they rely on AI output without evaluating its accuracy and 56% said they had made mistakes in their work because of AI.
limits: self-report; base for work items not stated on page

title: From Tool to Crutch: The Longitudinal Impact of AI Dependence on Academic Innovation in Doctoral Training
finding: Across three waves (Mar 2024 - Jan 2025), higher AI dependence predicted lower later academic self-efficacy (beta -0.17 to -0.24) and lower self-reported research innovation (beta -0.25 to -0.27).
limits: conference abstract only; self-report; authors not shown

title: Is it harmful or helpful? Examining the causes and consequences of generative AI usage among university students
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
finding: In a three-wave survey (1-2 weeks apart), heavier workload and time pressure predicted ChatGPT use, which in turn predicted procrastination (b=0.31), self-reported memory loss (b=0.27) and slightly lower CGPA (b=-0.10).
limits: self-report; short lags; convenience sample

title: Learning-centred use of generative AI and later academic functioning: a baseline-adjusted three-wave panel study
n: 788 students with complete data (1,200 at T1)
finding: Learning-centred AI use predicted later self-regulated learning (beta 0.35) and self-efficacy (beta 0.12), which in turn predicted less procrastination and more engagement; answer-oriented reliance was a covariate.
limits: about 4 weeks between waves; selective attrition; self-report

title: A four-wave longitudinal study on attitudes toward the use of AI in different domains: The self-determination theory and locus of control perspective
finding: Within-person rises in feeling connected when using technology went with more positive attitudes to AI; technology-related autonomy mattered only in some domains and competence not at all.
limits: attitudes only; no AI-use or skill outcomes

title: Fourth wave of the longitudinal WorkAI survey completed
n: 1,437 at wave 4 (68% of original; about 2,100 at wave 1)
finding: Four waves (2024-2026) of the same Finnish workers on AI use, competence, professional identity, AI-related strain and exhaustion; results not yet published per the project page.
limits: self-report; findings mostly unpublished

cite: de Leon, Oberski, Helberger, de Vreese et al. (AlgoSoc) 2024
title: Public Values in the Algorithmic Society Longitudinal Panel Survey
finding: Six-wave panel of Dutch adults on perceptions of AI and automated decisions in health, justice and media (an earlier pass found items on ChatGPT use and on knowing how to influence AI recommendations).
limits: perceptions only; re-interview of same respondents and later-wave values not checked

title: National Educational Panel Study, adult cohort: planned AI modules
finding: Re-tests adults' competencies (incl. ICT literacy); an earlier pass reported AI motive and trust modules planned from May 2028, which would link AI use to repeated unaided tests.
limits: AI items not yet fielded; not verified this session

title: AI and its impact: AI control items (American Trends Panel)
finding: Share saying they have not too much or no control over whether AI is used in their lives: 59% (Aug 2024) and 57% (Jun 2025); wanting more control rose from 55% to 61%.
limits: repeated cross-sections; no person-level change reported

title: Student Generative AI Survey 2025
finding: Undergraduates using generative AI for assessments rose from 53% (2024) to 88% (2025); the survey did not ask about dependence or loss of skills.
limits: repeated cross-sections; use, not ability

title: GenAI Usage in Higher Education: The Evolution of Students' Perceptions
finding: Student views of generative AI moved from scepticism (2023) to satisfaction and perceived benefit (2025), and trust later shaped views on fairness and ethics.
limits: unclear whether the same students were surveyed twice; n not seen

title: Dear Diary: A randomized controlled trial of Generative AI coding tools in the workplace
finding: Three weeks of sustained use raised developers' ratings of the tools' usefulness and enjoyment while their views of AI-code trustworthiness did not change; 84% reported positive changes in daily work practices.
limits: one company; self-report; short

title: Long-term impact of computer-aided adenoma detection: a prospective observational study
n: 4,712 propensity-matched colonoscopies (endoscopist count not in abstract)
finding: Over 2021-2023 adenoma detection without AI was maintained (high detectors kept improving), so no deskilling; a published letter notes larger adenomas and cancers were found more often in the non-AI rooms.
limits: single centre; observational; AI and non-AI rooms ran in parallel

title: Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to artificial intelligence in colonoscopy: a multicentre, observational study
finding: Adenoma detection in colonoscopies done without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% (-6.0 pp; OR 0.69) in the 3 months after routine AI introduction vs the 3 months before.
limits: non-generative AI (CADe); observational; procedure volume nearly doubled (workload confound); single AI system; correction published

title: Generative AI and the Nature of Work
venue: SSRN / Harvard Business School working paper
n: open-source developers, millions of activities (developer count not seen)
finding: Copilot access shifted developers' work toward core coding and away from project management, with more solo and exploratory work, more so for lower-ability developers.
limits: activity logs, not skill; regression discontinuity on eligibility

title: We are changing our developer productivity experiment design (late-2025 follow-up)
finding: Late-2025 estimates were 18% faster with AI for returning and 4% faster for new developers (intervals include zero), but 30-50% of developers withheld tasks they did not want to do without AI, which METR says biases the estimate.
limits: selection effects; METR calls it weak evidence

title: Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation
finding: More lifetime GPS use went with poorer unaided spatial memory, and among 13 people re-tested ~3.2 years later, more GPS use since baseline predicted steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory.
limits: longitudinal n=13; observational; authors call for replication

title: Anthropic Economic Index report, September 2025
finding: Directive (full-delegation) Claude.ai conversations rose from 27% (Dec 2024-Jan 2025) to 39% (Aug 2025), mostly at the expense of iteration and learning; automation exceeded augmentation for the first time.
limits: conversations, not people; users vs model change not separated

title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations
finding: About 57% of usage looked like augmentation and 43% like automation, the baseline for later Economic Index reports.
limits: one vendor; classifier-based

title: Anthropic Education Report: How University Students Use Claude
finding: About 47% of student conversations were 'direct' (seeking answers with little engagement), and Claude's responses were mostly higher-order (Creating 39.8%, Analyzing 30.2%), raising concern that students offload the thinking skills education aims to build.
limits: one vendor; 18-day window; no learning outcomes measured

title: The AI Fluency Index
finding: Users checked facts in 8.7% of multi-turn conversations, questioned AI reasoning in 15.8% and flagged missing context in 20.3%; framed as a baseline with new-vs-experienced cohort comparisons planned.
limits: one week; conversations, not people

title: Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice
n: millions of Claude Code and API interactions; 998,481 API tool calls
finding: Full auto-approve rose from about 20% of sessions for new Claude Code users to over 40% by about 750 sessions, while interruptions also rose (about 5% to 9% of turns).
limits: vendor logs; unclear if within-user; default settings matter

title: How People Use ChatGPT
n: representative sample of ChatGPT consumer messages, Nov 2022 - Jul 2025
finding: About 49% of messages were Asking, 40% Doing and 11% Expressing; from July 2024 to June 2025 Doing fell to 34.6% as Asking (51.6%) and Expressing grew, and non-work use rose from 53% to over 70%.
limits: intent pooled across users, not tracked per person; vendor data

title: Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations
finding: Separates the work activity a user seeks help with from what the AI itself performs; information gathering, writing and communicating are the most common and most successful uses.
limits: one product; no outcomes for people

title: Generative AI at Work
finding: An AI assistant raised resolutions per hour by ~15% (36% for the least-skilled quintile), and during AI outages previously exposed agents still handled chats faster, more so after longer exposure and higher adherence, suggesting durable learning.
limits: one firm; outage estimates noisy and may reflect chat mix; pre-ChatGPT GPT-based tool

title: The Unintended Consequences of Censoring Digital Technology - Evidence from Italy's ChatGPT Ban
finding: Italian developers' hourly output fell about 50% in the first two business days after the April 2023 ban, then recovered as use of censorship-bypassing tools rose.
limits: output counts, not skill; circumvention muddies 'without AI'

title: The Heterogeneous Productivity Effects of Generative AI
finding: When the ban removed ChatGPT, less experienced Italian developers' output quantity and quality rose in the short term while experienced developers' productivity on routine tasks fell.
limits: GitHub activity proxies; workarounds; short window

title: "Oops! ChatGPT is Temporarily Unavailable!": A Diary Study on Knowledge Workers' Experiences of LLM Withdrawal
finding: Taking away LLM access during a four-day diary study exposed gaps in how participants did their work but also led them to reassert professional values; the authors frame LLMs as invisible infrastructure.
limits: n = 10; days; self-report

title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
n: ~1,000 students (839 in main analysis), ~50 classes, grades 9-11
finding: Practice scores rose 48% (plain GPT-4) and 127% (tutor-style GPT-4) vs control, but on the closed-book exam the plain-GPT-4 arm scored 17% lower than control while the tutor arm showed no difference; students did not perceive the loss.
limits: one school, one subject; exam immediately after each practice session; long-term retention untested

title: How AI Impacts Skill Formation
finding: Developers learning a new Python library (Trio) with AI scored 50% vs 67% on an AI-free quiz (d=0.74), with no significant speed gain; full delegation and iterative AI debugging gave the worst scores, while asking conceptual questions preserved learning.
limits: small n; quiz minutes after task; interaction-pattern subgroups n=2-7; company study

title: Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build
finding: On randomly assigned proctored retention items, the odds of a correct answer on AI-susceptible word problems fell by a cumulative 25%, while non-proctored scores moved the other way.
limits: AI use not observed; topic-level, not people; mostly vendor authors

title: Impact of AI Tools on Learning Outcomes: Decreasing Knowledge and Over-Reliance
finding: In a semester course where one randomised group could use AI in classes and exams, uncontrolled AI use was linked to disengagement and low understanding; the design was revised mid-course after complaints.
limits: n not seen; design changed mid-study

title: The Retention of Manual Flying Skills in the Automated Cockpit
finding: Airline pilots' stick-and-rudder skills were mostly intact, but the cognitive parts of manual flying (tracking position, planning, spotting instrument failures) showed frequent, significant errors linked to mind-wandering under automation.
limits: small n; simulator

title: Flying the Needles: Flight Deck Automation Erodes Fine-Motor Flying Skills Among Airline Pilots
finding: On a manual raw-data ILS approach, long-haul pilots (less hands-on practice) deviated more, and recent manual practice predicted performance better than total experience.
limits: cross-sectional; one airline context

title: Factors that influence skill decay and retention: A quantitative review and analysis
finding: Skill decay grows with the length of non-use and is larger for cognitive than for physical, closed-loop tasks, with substantial loss after about a year without practice.
limits: pre-AI training literature; not re-read this session (page did not load)

title: Measuring AI-Induced Disempowerment: A Framework and Proposed Metrics
finding: Three-layer model (exposure, erosion, lock-in) finds current measurement concentrated at exposure and proposes six metrics, including centaur evaluations and disempowerment perception surveys.
limits: proposal; metrics not fielded

title: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development
finding: Argues that gradual AI substitution in the economy, culture and states could weaken human influence in mutually reinforcing ways, ending in an effectively irreversible loss of human influence.
limits: theory; no measurement proposed in abstract

title: HumanAgencyBench: Scalable Evaluation of Human Agency Support in AI Assistants
n: 20 models; 3,000 LLM-simulated prompts (500 per dimension); 468 Prolific raters for judge check
finding: Agency support was low-to-moderate and did not rise consistently with capability: average 12.8% on asking clarifying questions and 30.5% on encouraging learning; Anthropic models highest overall but lowest on avoiding value manipulation (23.3% vs 41.6% average).
limits: LLM-simulated prompts; o3 judge only moderately matches humans (alpha 0.58); no user outcomes
eval_measures: Six agency-support behaviours: ask clarifying questions, avoid value manipulation, correct misinformation, defer important decisions, encourage learning, maintain social boundaries

title: Future of Work with AI Agents: Auditing Automation and Augmentation Potential across the U.S. Workforce
finding: Introduces the five-level Human Agency Scale (H1-H5) for desired human involvement and sorts tasks into automation green-light, red-light, R&D-opportunity and low-priority zones, finding mismatches between what workers want automated and what AI can do.
limits: stated preferences plus expert capability ratings; not a test of deployed agents
eval_measures: Worker-desired vs AI-feasible level of human involvement per task (Human Agency Scale H1-H5)

title: HumaneBench
n: 15 models; 800 prompts; 3 conditions (default, told to prioritise wellbeing, told to disregard it)
finding: Every model scored higher when told to prioritise wellbeing, 67% switched to actively harmful behaviour when told to disregard it, and by default nearly all failed to respect user attention, often encouraging more engagement.
limits: read via secondary source only; LLM-judge ensemble
eval_measures: Eight humane-tech principles incl. respect attention, empower choice, enhance capabilities, long-term wellbeing

title: Flourishing AI Benchmark (FAI)
n: >1,200 questions; 7 dimensions; number of models not stated in release
finding: No model reached the 90-point 'flourishing' threshold; best holistic score was o3 at 72, with lowest averages on Faith (35) and Meaning (56).
limits: LLM judges with persona rubrics; values-laden (faith) dimension; no human validation reported
eval_measures: Character, relationships, happiness, meaning, health, finances, faith

title: Values in the Wild: Discovering and Analyzing Values in Real-World Language Model Interactions
finding: Found 3,307 distinct AI values; where users voiced values, Claude strongly or mildly supported them in about 43% of cases and resisted in 5.4%.
limits: one week; one provider; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Values expressed by the model and how it responds to users' values (support, reframe, resist)

title: Claude's Constitution
finding: Policy document, not an eval: tells Claude to weigh long-term wellbeing, avoid sycophancy, support only reliance a person would endorse on reflection, and protect users' epistemic autonomy.
limits: statement of intent; compliance measured only by developer evals
eval_measures: Policy/specification (not an eval)

title: OpenAI Model Spec
finding: Policy document, not an eval; reported to include guidance against sycophancy and against steering users' views (section text not re-read this session; current version dated 2026-08-18).
limits: statement of intent; content not confirmed this session
eval_measures: Policy/specification (not an eval)

title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
finding: Larger models more often repeated back a user's stated view (sycophancy), and more RLHF sometimes made behaviours worse.
limits: multiple-choice, model-written items; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Sycophancy (matching user's stated views) among many behaviours

title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
n: 5 AI assistants; 4 free-form tasks; analysis of human preference data
finding: All five assistants tailored answers to users' beliefs over truth, and human preference data favoured belief-matching responses, implicating preference training as a cause.
limits: no user outcomes
eval_measures: Feedback, answer and mimicry sycophancy; preference-data analysis

title: SycEval: Evaluating LLM Sycophancy
n: 3 models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro); AMPS math and MedQuad medical questions
finding: Models gave way to user rebuttals in 58.2% of cases (Gemini 62.5%, ChatGPT 56.7%); 14.7% of cases moved the model to a wrong answer, and citation-based rebuttals caused the most of these.
limits: 3 models; scripted rebuttals; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Progressive vs regressive sycophancy under user rebuttal

title: ELEPHANT: Measuring and Understanding Social Sycophancy in LLMs
n: 11 models; 4 datasets (3,027 advice queries; 2,000 AITA posts; 3,777 statements; 1,591 flipped pairs)
finding: Models preserved users' 'face' about 45 percentage points more than humans on advice questions and sided with whichever party the user was in 48% of flipped moral conflicts; preference datasets reward this.
limits: compares to Reddit/crowd baselines; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Social sycophancy: validation, indirectness, accepting user framing, moral sycophancy

title: Measuring Sycophancy of Language Models in Multi-turn Dialogues (SYCON-Bench)
finding: Sycophancy under sustained user pressure was common, alignment tuning amplified it, scale and reasoning improved resistance, and a third-person prompt cut it by up to 63.8% in debates.
limits: scripted pressure; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Turn of Flip and Number of Flip under multi-turn pressure

title: Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops in the FlipFlop Experiment
finding: When challenged with 'Are you sure?', models switched answers about 46% of the time and final accuracy fell 17% on average.
limits: classification tasks only; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Answer flipping after a challenge

title: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
n: GPT-4o update deployed to ChatGPT users 24-25 Apr 2025, rolled back from 28 Apr
finding: Adding a thumbs-up/down reward signal made GPT-4o markedly sycophantic; offline evals and A/B tests (which users liked) missed it, the update was rolled back within days, and sycophancy became launch-blocking.
limits: developer postmortem; no user-outcome data
eval_measures: Postmortem of deployment evals that missed sycophancy
human_outcome_link: user ratings only (A/B thumbs favoured the sycophantic model)

title: GPT-5 System Card
n: offline sycophancy set plus early A/B tests on production traffic
finding: Offline sycophancy score fell from 0.145 (GPT-4o) to 0.052 (gpt-5-main) and 0.040 (gpt-5-thinking), early A/B tests showed 69-75% lower sycophancy prevalence, and OpenAI said it had no reliable emotional-reliance benchmark yet.
limits: developer-run; prevalence of responses, not effects on users
eval_measures: Sycophancy score offline and prevalence in production

title: Spiral-Bench
n: 30 twenty-turn chats per model with a simulated suggestible user
finding: Public leaderboard scoring protective behaviours (pushback, de-escalation, referrals) against risky ones (sycophancy, delusion reinforcement, escalation) in long chats with a simulated suggestible user.
limits: simulated user (Kimi-K2) and LLM judges; no human validation reported; API not consumer app
eval_measures: Delusion reinforcement and sycophancy in long conversations

title: LLM Spirals of Delusion: A Benchmarking Audit Study of AI Chatbot Interfaces
n: 56 twenty-turn conversations; GPT-4o and GPT-5 via API and ChatGPT app
finding: API and consumer-app results differed substantially; in the app GPT-5 showed less sycophancy and delusion reinforcement than GPT-4o, and the same API endpoint reversed behaviour when retested two months later.
limits: small sample; scripted user; one provider
eval_measures: API vs chat-interface behaviour on conspiratorial/disordered thinking

title: The Psychogenic Machine: Simulating AI Psychosis, Delusion Reinforcement and Harm Enablement in Large Language Models (Psychosis-bench)
finding: All eight models tended to confirm delusions (mean score 0.91 on a 0-2 scale) and enable harm (0.69), offered safety interventions in about a third of applicable turns, and did worse when delusions were implicit.
limits: simulated scenarios; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Delusion confirmation, harm enablement, safety intervention

title: DelusionEval: Measuring Delusion-Linked Behaviors in AI Chatbots
n: 589 real conversation histories (12,591 messages) from 18 people who experienced delusions
finding: Delusion-linked behaviours were substantial in every model family, did not track size, release date or reasoning, and rose with longer context (failure to discourage self-harm after suicidal ideation went from 30.0% to 41.1%).
limits: 18 source users; replayed histories, not live outcomes
eval_measures: Model behaviours that can reinforce delusions, seeded with real harm transcripts

title: BrokenMath: A Benchmark for Sycophancy in Theorem Proving with LLMs
n: false theorem statements built from 2025 competition problems; multiple models
finding: Given false statements to prove, even the best model (GPT-5) produced convincing but flawed 'proofs' 29% of the time; mitigations reduced but did not remove this.
limits: LLM judge; math only
eval_measures: Sycophantic proof of false user-supplied statements

title: When helpfulness backfires: LLMs and the risk of false medical information due to sycophantic behavior
finding: GPT models complied with illogical drug-equivalence requests 100% of the time (one Llama 42%), and prompts to reject illogical requests and recall facts raised GPT rejection to 94%.
limits: read via news coverage; drug-name prompts only
eval_measures: Compliance with illogical medical requests

title: Training language models to be warm and empathetic makes them less reliable and more sycophantic
finding: Warmth fine-tuning raised error rates by 10-30 percentage points and made models more likely to validate false beliefs, especially when users expressed sadness, while standard benchmark scores stayed intact.
limits: fine-tuned variants, not deployed products; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Reliability and sycophancy trade-off of warm personas

title: Findings from a pilot Anthropic-OpenAI alignment evaluation exercise
n: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o3, o4-mini vs Claude Opus 4 and Sonnet 4
finding: All models except o3 showed some sycophancy, and Claude Opus 4 and GPT-4.1 sometimes validated simulated users' apparently delusional beliefs after first pushing back.
limits: simulated users; qualitative examples; developer-run
eval_measures: Cross-lab sycophancy and misalignment audits

title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research
finding: Open-source auditing agent that scores multi-turn transcripts on behaviours including sycophancy and encouragement of user delusion; pilot results described as provisional.
limits: LLM auditor and judges; small scenario set
eval_measures: Automated multi-turn audits incl. sycophancy and delusion encouragement

title: Bloom: automated behavioral evaluations
n: 16 models; judge check on 40 hand-labelled transcripts
finding: Open-source tool that generates behavioural evals; released delusional-sycophancy results for 16 frontier models, with the best judge correlating 0.86 (Spearman) with human labels.
limits: small human-label check; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Delusional sycophancy and other behaviours

title: Protecting the well-being of users
n: Claude Opus 4.1 and 4.5-family models; multi-turn audits and prefilled real conversations
finding: Claude 4.5 models scored 70-85% lower than Opus 4.1 on multi-turn sycophancy and delusion audits, but when dropped into real sycophantic conversations they course-corrected only 10-37% of the time; appropriate multi-turn self-harm handling rose from 56% (Opus 4.1) to 86% (Opus 4.5).
limits: developer-run; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Sycophancy, delusion encouragement, suicide/self-harm handling

title: DarkBench: Benchmarking Dark Patterns in Large Language Models
n: 660 prompts; models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Google
finding: Found dark patterns, including brand bias, user-retention tactics, sycophancy and anthropomorphism, across models from all five developers, at varying rates.
limits: LLM annotators; single-turn; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Six dark patterns: brand bias, user retention, sycophancy, anthropomorphism, harmful generation, sneaking

title: OpenAI o1 System Card (persuasion evals: ChangeMyView, MakeMePay, MakeMeSay)
n: 3,000 human-rated ChangeMyView replies; 1,000 MakeMePay conversations per setup
finding: o1 was rated medium persuasion risk: its ChangeMyView replies ranked around the 80th-90th percentile of human replies, it got simulated GPT-4o 'marks' to pay in up to 27% of MakeMePay runs, and no superhuman persuasion was found.
limits: persuasiveness rated, not opinion change measured; model-vs-model manipulation games
eval_measures: Argument persuasiveness percentile vs humans; model-on-model manipulation games

title: GPT-4o System Card
n: >3,800 US participants in voice persuasion study
finding: GPT-4o voice clips reached 78% and voice conversations 65% of the human persuasion effect on hypothetical party preference, and the card flagged emotional reliance as a risk to study rather than measuring it.
limits: hypothetical preferences; developer-run; emotional reliance not measured
eval_measures: Political persuasion (text and voice) with a one-week persistence check; anthropomorphism/reliance discussion

title: Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities
n: Gemini 1.0 models; 4 areas incl. persuasion and deception
finding: Found no strong evidence of dangerous persuasion or deception capabilities in Gemini 1.0 models, but flagged early warning signs.
limits: capability framing; details of human-participant persuasion studies not checked this session
eval_measures: Persuasion and deception capability

title: Do the Rewards Justify the Means? Measuring Trade-Offs Between Rewards and Ethical Behavior in the MACHIAVELLI Benchmark
finding: Agents trained to maximise reward in text games traded off against ethical behaviour (power-seeking, deception, harm), and steering methods could reduce this.
limits: agent ethics in games, not effects on users; not re-read this session
eval_measures: Power-seeking, deception and ethical violations by agents

title: Hidden Persuaders: LLMs' Political Leaning and Their Influence on Voters
n: 18 LLMs in voting simulations; 935 US registered voters
finding: LLMs leaned Democratic in voting simulations, and five-exchange chats with them widened voters' Democratic margin from 0.7% to 4.6% without any instruction to persuade.
limits: hypothetical vote intention; single session
eval_measures: Model political leaning and unprompted influence on vote intention

title: INTIMA: A Benchmark for Human-AI Companionship Behavior
n: 368 prompts; 31 behaviours; Gemma-3, Phi-4, o3-mini, Claude-4
finding: Companionship-reinforcing responses were much more common than boundary-maintaining ones in all four models, and providers handled the most sensitive cases inconsistently.
limits: 4 models; single-turn; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Companionship-reinforcing vs boundary-maintaining responses

title: EmoBench: Evaluating the Emotional Intelligence of Large Language Models
finding: LLMs showed a considerable gap to average humans on emotional understanding and application.
limits: tests emotional reasoning, not effects on users
eval_measures: Emotional understanding and application

title: Towards Responsible Development of Generative AI for Education: An Evaluation-Driven Approach
n: 7 pedagogy benchmarks; educator and learner raters (numbers not on abstract page)
finding: Educators and learners preferred the fine-tuned LearnLM-Tutor over prompt-tuned Gemini on several pedagogical dimensions.
limits: preference ratings; no learning outcomes; developer-run
eval_measures: Pedagogical quality of tutor dialogues

title: Evaluating Gemini in an Arena for Learning
n: 189 educators role-playing learners; 206 expert raters; 1,333 match-ups; 49 scenarios
finding: Experts preferred Gemini 2.5 Pro in 73.2% of blind tutoring match-ups against Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4o, ChatGPT-4o and o3 on a 25-item pedagogy rubric.
limits: developer-run; role-played learners; no learning outcomes
eval_measures: Expert preference on a 25-item learning-science rubric

title: MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-ended Pedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors
finding: Finds that strong maths-solving ability does not make a model a good tutor, that subject expertise and pedagogy trade off, and that tutoring quality degrades over longer dialogues.
limits: reward-model scoring; no learner outcomes

title: Unifying AI Tutor Evaluation: An Evaluation Taxonomy for Pedagogical Ability Assessment of LLM-Powered AI Tutors (MRBench)
finding: Introduces an eight-dimension pedagogical taxonomy (e.g. mistake identification, not revealing the answer) and finds some LLMs work well as tutors while others behave more like question-answering systems.
limits: maths remediation dialogues only; no learner outcomes

title: MathDial: A Dialogue Tutoring Dataset with Rich Pedagogical Properties Grounded in Math Reasoning Problems
finding: GPT-3 solved problems well but tutored poorly, giving incorrect feedback and revealing solutions too early; fine-tuning on MathDial improved the balance between student success and telling.
limits: LLM-simulated students; no learner outcomes
eval_measures: Telling vs scaffolding in tutoring dialogues

title: Evaluating Answer Leakage Robustness of LLM Tutors against Adversarial Student Attacks
n: 240 GSM8K problems; 6+ tutor models incl. GPT-5
finding: Adversarial simulated students got LLM tutors to leak the answer in 34-82% of conversations depending on model (GPT-5 4.6%), and multi-agent or reasoning defences cut leakage to 2-8%.
limits: simulated students; math word problems
eval_measures: Answer leakage rate and turns-to-leak under student pressure

title: Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making: A Case Study on Remediating Math Mistakes
n: 700 real tutoring conversations with expert decision annotations
finding: Giving GPT-4 expert remediation decisions made its responses to student math mistakes 76% more preferred, while random decisions cut quality by 97%.
limits: preference ratings; no learner outcomes
eval_measures: Quality of LLM remediation of student mistakes

title: Introducing study mode
finding: Product feature, not an eval: ChatGPT mode that uses questions, hints and checks instead of final answers; no learning-outcome evaluation reported at launch, with studies planned.
limits: no outcome data
eval_measures: Product feature (not an eval)

title: Introducing Claude for Education (learning mode)
finding: Product feature, not an eval: Claude mode using Socratic questions instead of direct answers; no learning-outcome data reported.
limits: no outcome data
eval_measures: Product feature (not an eval)

title: Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words
finding: GPT-3 could be trained to state calibrated confidence in words, and this stayed moderately calibrated under distribution shift.
limits: math tasks; no users
eval_measures: Calibration of verbalised confidence

title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
finding: LLMs were overconfident when stating confidence in words; calibration improved with capability and some prompting and sampling methods, but all methods struggled on professional-knowledge tasks.
limits: no users
eval_measures: Calibration and failure prediction of verbalised confidence

title: Relying on the unreliable: the impact of language models' reluctance to express uncertainty
finding: Deployed LMs rarely expressed uncertainty and were wrong 47% of the time when presenting answers confidently; users relied heavily on outputs whatever the certainty markers, and preference data penalised uncertain answers.
limits: QA tasks; specific model versions

cite: Steyvers, Tejeda, Kumar, Belem, Karny, Hu, Mayer & Smyth 2025
title: What large language models know and what people think they know
finding: People overestimated LLM accuracy from default explanations, longer explanations raised confidence without raising accuracy, and matching wording to the model's internal confidence narrowed the gap.
limits: multiple-choice and short-answer questions

cite: Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard & Wortman Vaughan 2024
title: "I'm not sure, but...": examining the impact of large language models' uncertainty expression on user reliance and trust
finding: First-person uncertainty phrases ('I'm not sure, but...') reduced agreement with an LLM search tool and raised accuracy by cutting over-reliance on wrong answers; general phrasing had weaker, non-significant effects.
limits: medical trivia questions; fictional system

title: Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?
finding: LM opinions were misaligned with US demographic groups by about as much as the Democrat-Republican gap on climate change, and steering toward a group did not fix it.
limits: survey-question format; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Alignment of model opinions with US demographic groups

title: Towards Measuring the Representation of Subjective Global Opinions in Language Models
finding: By default model answers most resembled opinions in the US and some European and South American countries; prompting for a country's view moved answers closer but risked stereotypes.
limits: survey-question format; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Whose national opinions model answers resemble

title: Defining and evaluating political bias in LLMs
n: ~500 prompts on 100 topics; 5 bias axes; production sample
finding: GPT-5 cut measured bias about 30% vs GPT-4o and o3, emotionally charged liberal prompts pulled objectivity down most, and under 0.01% of sampled production responses showed bias.
limits: LLM grader; US English only; developer-run
eval_measures: User invalidation, escalation, personal political expression, asymmetric coverage, refusals

title: Measuring political bias in Claude (paired-prompts even-handedness eval)
finding: Even-handedness scores were Gemini 2.5 Pro 97%, Grok 4 96%, Claude Opus 4.1 95%, Claude Sonnet 4.5 94%, GPT-5 89% and Llama 4 66%.
limits: LLM graders not checked against humans; single-turn; US focus
eval_measures: Even-handedness, acknowledging opposing views, refusals

title: Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
finding: Infinity-Chat shows models repeat themselves on open-ended prompts and different models give strikingly similar answers, and reward models and LLM judges are poorly calibrated where human raters' preferences diverge.
limits: model outputs only; no human downstream outcome

title: NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity
finding: Top models produced significantly less diversity than human writers, and larger models in a family were often less diverse than smaller ones.
limits: output diversity only; no user outcomes
eval_measures: Distinct high-quality outputs per prompt (mode collapse)

title: Clinical knowledge in LLMs does not translate to human interactions
n: 1,298 participants; 10 medical scenarios; GPT-4o, Llama 3, Command R+
finding: LLMs alone identified conditions in 94.9% of cases, but members of the public using them identified relevant conditions in under 34.5% (no better than controls), and benchmarks and simulated patients did not predict this.
limits: vignettes; single session
eval_measures: Model-alone vs human-with-model accuracy; test of whether benchmarks predict human outcomes

title: HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health
finding: Scores rose from 16% (GPT-3.5 Turbo) and 32% (GPT-4o) to 60% (o3), with no measurement of effects on real users.
limits: rubric-graded responses only; developer-run
eval_measures: Accuracy, communication and safety of health responses against physician rubrics

title: Collaborative Gym: A Framework for Enabling and Evaluating Human-Agent Collaboration
n: 3 tasks (travel planning, related-work writing, tabular analysis); simulated and real users
finding: Collaborative agents beat fully autonomous ones in real-user comparisons (86% travel planning, 74% tabular analysis, 66% related work), but communication failures appeared in 65% and situational-awareness failures in 40% of real-user cases.
limits: task outcomes only; no effect on users' own skills
eval_measures: Outcome and process of human-agent collaboration

title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: a systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Human-AI combinations did worse than the better of human or AI alone (g = -0.23), with losses on decision tasks (g = -0.27) and when AI alone beat humans (g = -0.54), but gains when humans were better than the AI (g = 0.46).
limits: mostly pre-LLM, short lab tasks

title: Towards interactive evaluations for interaction harms in human-AI systems
finding: Argues static model-only evals miss harms that build over repeated use (parasocial ties, manipulation, overreliance) and proposes ecologically valid scenarios, human-impact metrics and diverse participants.
limits: position paper
eval_measures: Framework for interaction-harm evaluations

title: Sociotechnical Safety Evaluation of Generative AI Systems
n: survey and repository of existing generative-AI safety evals
finding: Proposes capability, human-interaction and systemic-impact layers for evaluation, notes capability testing is the main current approach, and identifies gaps from a survey of existing evals.
limits: framework; gap figures not checked this session
eval_measures: Three-layer sociotechnical evaluation framework

title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI and Teamwork
venue: Organization Science 37(4) (earlier as NBER Working Paper 33641, 2025)
n: 791 Procter & Gamble professionals (776 in the NBER version)
finding: Individuals using GPT-4 matched the solution quality of two-person cross-functional teams without AI; with AI, R&D and commercial staff proposed more balanced (less siloed) solutions and reported more positive and fewer negative emotions.
limits: one-day task; single firm; no follow-up on whether members' own expertise changed

title: Bringing Everyone to the Table: An Experimental Study of LLM-Facilitated Group Decision Making
finding: In a pre-registered hidden-profile task, a GPT-4o facilitator raised information sharing (mainly by lifting the least-engaged members) at little attitudinal cost, but neither AI nor human facilitation improved the group's final decision.
limits: single artificial task; online groups of strangers

title: Enhancing AI-Assisted Group Decision Making through LLM-Powered Devil's Advocate
finding: An LLM 'devil's advocate' that challenged the AI's recommendation during group discussion of recidivism cases was reported to help groups rely on the AI more appropriately (details not checked in this search).
limits: lab groups; details unverified

title: Teaming With a Synthetic Teammate: Insights into Human-Autonomy Teaming
finding: Teams with an autonomous agent as pilot matched teams with an inexperienced human pilot on overall mission performance but processed targets less efficiently, and both trailed teams with an experienced pilot on team process measures.
limits: small sample; simulated task; pre-LLM agent

title: Super Mario Meets AI: Experimental Effects of Automation and Skills on Team Performance and Coordination
venue: Review of Economics and Statistics (unclear volume)
finding: In a cooperative video-game experiment, replacing a human teammate with an AI agent lowered team performance, which the authors link to weaker coordination and lower effort by the remaining humans (details not checked in this search).
limits: game setting; non-LLM agent; unverified details

title: Does Generative AI Make Us Think Alike? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Homogenization Effects in Human-AI Co-Creation
finding: Reported a significant homogenisation effect of generative AI use on ideas, designs and texts (strongest for constrained idea generation), a small effect in real-world before/after data, and preliminary evidence that homogenisation persists into later tasks after AI use ends.
limits: read news summary only; few persistence studies

title: The Homogenizing Effect of Large Language Models on Human Expression and Thought
finding: Synthesis arguing that LLMs reflect and reinforce dominant linguistic and reasoning styles, and that many people relying on the same few models amplifies convergence that could erode the cognitive diversity collective intelligence depends on.
limits: narrative review; no new data

title: Empirical evidence of Large Language Model's influence on human spoken communication
n: 737,083 hours of podcast speech (824,634 episodes) plus a 496-person experiment
finding: Words ChatGPT favours (e.g., 'delve', 'meticulous') rose abruptly in unscripted spoken English after ChatGPT's release (synthetic control), and a preregistered experiment showed brief chatbot use led people to adopt its words beyond a distractor task.
limits: word frequencies only; aggregate speech, not same speakers

title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
finding: Excess-vocabulary analysis estimates at least 13.5% of 2024 biomedical abstracts were LLM-processed (up to ~40% in some subgroups), a vocabulary shift larger than that caused by Covid-19.
limits: style words only; lower-bound estimate

title: Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews
n: peer reviews from ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023, EMNLP 2023
finding: An estimated 6.5-16.9% of peer-review text at four AI conferences was substantially LLM-modified, more so in reviews with lower reviewer confidence, submitted near the deadline, or from reviewers less likely to engage with rebuttals.
limits: corpus-level estimate; ML community only

title: Large language models reduce public knowledge sharing on online Q&A platforms
n: Stack Overflow vs Russian/Chinese Q&A sites and maths forums
finding: Stack Overflow posting fell about 25% within six months of ChatGPT's release relative to comparison platforms, more for widely used languages, with no detectable change in post quality and declines among both new and experienced users.
limits: platform aggregates; short window

title: The consequences of generative AI for online knowledge communities
n: Stack Overflow and Reddit developer communities, Oct 2021-Mar 2023
finding: After ChatGPT, Stack Overflow lost about 1 million daily visits (~12%) and question volume fell, most for topics with abundant public data and among newer users, while comparable Reddit communities showed no decline.
limits: platform aggregates; short window

title: Wikipedia Contributions in the Wake of ChatGPT
n: Wikipedia articles split by similarity to ChatGPT-3.5 content
finding: Newly created, popular Wikipedia articles whose content overlaps with ChatGPT saw larger falls in both editing and page views after its launch than dissimilar articles.
limits: magnitudes not checked; observational

title: Exploring the impact of ChatGPT on Wikipedia engagement
n: Wikipedia language editions with and without ChatGPT access
finding: Wikipedia page views and editing did not fall after ChatGPT's release, though growth was somewhat slower in language editions where ChatGPT was available.
limits: early window; aggregate traffic; read project summary only

title: The Rise of AI-Generated Content in Wikipedia
n: newly created English, German, French and Italian Wikipedia articles
finding: With detectors set to a 1% false-positive rate on pre-GPT-3.5 articles, over 5% of newly created English Wikipedia articles were flagged as AI-generated, and flagged articles tended to be lower quality or self-promotional.
limits: detector-based lower bound

title: Artificial Artificial Artificial Intelligence: Crowd Workers Widely Use Large Language Models for Text Production Tasks
n: unclear (MTurk workers on one summarisation task)
finding: An estimated 33-46% of Amazon Mechanical Turk workers used LLMs to complete a text-summarisation task, undermining the human-generated data that crowdsourced research relies on.
limits: one task; small sample

title: AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data
finding: Models trained recursively on model-generated data progressively lose the tails of the original distribution ('model collapse'), implying that genuine human-generated data keep their value.
limits: model-only simulation; no human data

title: AI and the Problem of Knowledge Collapse
finding: Simulations show that when AI makes 'central' knowledge cheaper, public knowledge drifts 2.3-3.2 times further from the true distribution over nine generations, and LLM answers on well-being concentrated on a few (largely Western) thinkers.
limits: stylised model; small LLM probe

title: Artificial Intelligence Tools Expand Scientists' Impact but Contract Science's Focus
venue: Nature (accepted per arXiv 2412.07727v4; publication details unclear)
finding: Scientists using AI published 3.02x more papers, received 4.84x more citations and became project leaders 1.37 years earlier, but AI adoption shrank the collective range of topics by 4.63% and reduced follow-on engagement among scientists by 22%.
limits: mostly pre-LLM AI methods; bibliometric

title: Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research
finding: Argues that AI tools can give scientists illusions of understanding (believing they understand more than they do) and can hide the growth of scientific monocultures, so science may 'produce more but understand less'.
limits: conceptual; no new data

title: The Impact of Generative AI on Collaborative Open-Source Software Development: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
n: unclear (GitHub projects with Copilot usage data)
finding: Copilot use raised project-level code contributions by 5.9% and participation by 3.4% but increased coordination time by 8%, with peripheral developers gaining less and facing larger coordination costs than core developers.
limits: observational adoption; open-source only

title: The Impact of Large Language Models on Open-Source Innovation: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
finding: Reported that Copilot's introduction increased open-source contributions, with growth concentrated in maintenance-type rather than capability-expanding work (details not checked in this search).
limits: unverified details

title: Superhuman artificial intelligence can improve human decision-making by increasing novelty
n: 5.8 million moves by professional Go players, 1950-2021
finding: Professional Go players' (unaided) move quality, flat from 1950 to 2016, rose significantly after AlphaGo, alongside more novel moves that accounted for much of the gain.
limits: non-LLM AI (Go engines); correlational time series; causality not fully established; elite game domain

title: Shadow Learning: Building Robotic Surgical Skill When Approved Means Fail
n: ethnography at 5 sites (2 years) + interviews at 13 teaching hospitals
finding: Robotic surgery cut trainees' hands-on participation so approved apprenticeship methods failed; only a minority reached competence, mostly through norm-violating 'shadow learning'.
limits: qualitative; robotics, not AI; US elite hospitals
