title: Losing Touch: An Embodiment Perspective on Coordination in Robotic Surgery
finding: Reported that robot-mediated surgery separated the surgeon from direct touch and redistributed sensing and coordination work to other members of the surgical team (details not checked in this search).
limits: qualitative; unverified details

title: Don't Expect Juniors to Teach Senior Professionals to Use Generative AI: Emerging Technology Risks and Novice AI Risk Mitigation Tactics
n: about 78 junior BCG consultants (interviews; number unverified)
finding: Junior consultants' tactics for managing GPT-4 risks were novice-level (e.g., changing human routines rather than system design), challenging the assumption that juniors can teach seniors how to use a new technology.
limits: interviews; one firm; unverified details

title: Sharing is Caring: The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Motivation and Effort of Knowledge Sharing
finding: In an online experiment, GenAI implementation changed psychological ownership, reputation and codification costs, with both positive and negative effects on employees' intentions to share knowledge.
limits: intentions only; effect sizes not checked

title: Employees are using ChatGPT for advice - but is this a good thing?
n: small number of in-depth interviews (tech/digitalisation firms)
finding: Some employees found it easier to ask ChatGPT than senior colleagues (always polite, no careful phrasing needed), which the authors flag as a risk to mentoring and workplace knowledge sharing.
limits: small qualitative sample; short report

title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation
n: 5,734 participants plus a representative UK virtual citizens' assembly
finding: Group statements drafted by an LLM mediator (the 'Habermas Machine') were rated more informative, clear and unbiased than human mediators' statements, reduced within-group division, and still included dissenting views; results replicated in a virtual citizens' assembly.
limits: short online deliberations; long-run effects not tested

title: Fine-tuning language models to find agreement among humans with diverse preferences
n: unclear (participants rating statements on thousands of questions)
finding: A 70B model fine-tuned with a group-preference reward model produced consensus statements preferred over the best human-written opinions in more than 65% of comparisons; people whose opinions were left out were more likely to dissent.
limits: preference ratings only; no behaviour change

title: Leveraging AI for democratic discourse: Chat interventions can improve online political conversations at scale
finding: Real-time LLM rephrasing suggestions in conversations on a divisive issue improved partners' reported conversation quality, democratic reciprocity and tone without changing conversation content or policy attitudes.
limits: single conversation; online sample

title: AI-Mediated Communication: Definition, Research Agenda, and Ethical Considerations
finding: Defines AI-mediated communication (an agent modifying, augmenting or generating messages on a person's behalf) and argues it unsettles assumptions about who holds agency in interpersonal communication.
limits: conceptual

title: Opportunities and Risks of LLMs for Scalable Deliberation with Polis
n: pilot experiments on Polis conversation data
finding: Pilots with Claude suggest LLMs can help organisers run Polis deliberations, with summarisation most promising, but context limits markedly affect output quality and the authors set out risks of LLM use in deliberative systems.
limits: pilot evaluations; no participant outcomes

title: How large language models can reshape collective intelligence
finding: Perspective by 28 authors mapping how LLMs change how information is aggregated, accessed and shared, setting out benefits, risks (including homogenisation) and open research questions for collective intelligence.
limits: conceptual

title: Machine culture
finding: Perspective arguing that machines (recommenders, chatbots, generative models) now act on cultural evolution's variation, transmission and selection, and setting a research agenda for machine-mediated social learning.
limits: conceptual

title: Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations
finding: Decentralised populations of LLM agents spontaneously converged on shared conventions, developed strong collective biases even when no single agent was biased, and could be tipped to a new convention by a small committed minority.
limits: agents only; no humans

title: Algorithmic monoculture and social welfare
finding: Formal model showing that when many decision-makers adopt the same, individually more accurate algorithm, overall decision quality can fall relative to more diverse, independent judgements.
limits: theoretical

title: The Vicious Circles of Skill Erosion: A Case Study of Cognitive Automation
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
finding: Years of reliance on automated accounting software produced skill erosion that neither workers nor managers noticed, driven by complacency that weakened activity awareness, competence maintenance and output checking; an earlier HICSS 2018 paper describes deskilling surfacing when the automation was discontinued and methods of recovery.
limits: single case; pre-LLM rule-based automation; recovery details from paper title/earlier version only

title: To engage or not to engage with AI for critical judgments: how professionals deal with opacity when using AI for medical diagnosis
n: 3 radiology departments in one US hospital
finding: Only one of three radiology departments built 'interrogation' practices and folded opaque AI outputs into final diagnoses; the other two did not engage with the AI's results.
limits: one hospital; pre-LLM tools

title: When Knowledge Work and Analytical Technologies Collide: The Practices and Consequences of Black Boxing Algorithmic Technologies
finding: In a two-year ethnography, banker groups with split junior/senior roles 'black boxed' analytical algorithms (using them without understanding), which limited junior bankers' expertise development, whereas groups that co-constructed analyses stayed aware of how the algorithms worked.
limits: one bank; qualitative; pre-generative tools

title: In the Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man Is King: Knowledge Brokerage in the Age of Learning Algorithms
n: Dutch police predictive-policing unit (ethnography; n unclear)
finding: In an ethnography of predictive policing, intelligence officers who brokered between the algorithm and frontline officers increasingly interpreted, selected and supplemented its outputs, so practical control over the knowledge shifted to these brokers.
limits: one force; qualitative; details not rechecked (page rate-limited)

title: When the Machine Meets the Expert: An Ethnography of Developing AI for Hiring
n: AI developers and HR professionals in one multinational (n unclear)
finding: Developers who set out to replace HR experts' judgment with a machine-learning hiring tool ended up, through mutual learning, building a hybrid practice that reintroduced HR expertise into the system.
limits: one firm; qualitative; not rechecked this session

title: Algorithms at Work: The New Contested Terrain of Control
finding: Review identifies six mechanisms of algorithmic control at work (restricting, recommending, recording, rating, replacing, rewarding) through which employers direct, evaluate and discipline workers, and documents worker resistance ('algoactivism').
limits: review; mostly pre-generative AI

title: The Theory of Technology Dominance: Understanding the Impact of Intelligent Decision Aids on Decision Makers' Judgments
finding: Proposes that reliance on intelligent decision aids depends on user experience, task complexity, familiarity with the aid and cognitive fit, and that long-term reliance can deskill users and stall novices' development of expertise.
limits: theory; expert-system era

title: The Impact of Outsourcing New Technologies on Integrative Capabilities and Performance
n: US banks adopting online banking (n unclear)
finding: Banks that outsourced their online-banking technology built weaker integrative capabilities and gained less performance benefit than banks that developed it in-house, an analogue for organisational capability loss through outsourcing.
limits: outsourcing analogy, not AI; not rechecked

title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
finding: By mid-2026, employment of 22-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations was ~19% below its counterfactual, driven by reduced hiring and concentrated where AI substitutes rather than complements work, with no comparable gap for experienced workers.
limits: descriptive, not causal; employment not skill; weakens with education controls

title: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from U.S. Resume and Job Posting Data
finding: From 2023Q1, junior employment in firms that began posting 'AI integrator' roles fell sharply relative to non-adopters while senior employment kept rising, driven mainly by slower junior hiring rather than more separations, with mid-tier graduates hit hardest.
limits: adoption proxied by job postings; resume-data coverage

title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects (revised as 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI')
n: Danish adoption surveys linked to administrative records (exact n not on page read)
finding: Two years after ChatGPT's launch, chatbot adoption had null effects on earnings and recorded hours at worker and workplace level (effects above 2% ruled out), while employers reorganised tasks and created new work in content generation, AI oversight and AI integration.
limits: early period; exposed occupations only

title: Firm Investments in Artificial Intelligence Technologies and Changes in Workforce Composition
finding: Firms investing in (pre-generative) AI shifted toward more educated, STEM- and IT-specialised workforces and flatter hierarchies, with a rising share of junior workers and falling shares of middle-management and senior roles.
limits: 2010s AI; correlational

title: Artificial Intelligence and Jobs: Evidence from Online Vacancies
finding: Establishments with AI-exposed task structures hired more AI workers and reduced hiring for non-AI positions in 2010-2018, with no detectable aggregate effects at occupation or industry level.
limits: pre-generative AI; vacancy data

title: Tracking Firm Use of AI in Real Time: A Snapshot from the Business Trends and Outlook Survey
n: US businesses in the Census Bureau's biweekly BTOS
finding: Firm AI use rose from 3.7% to 5.4% (Sep 2023-Feb 2024); few AI users reported cutting employment, and many reorganised by training staff, redesigning workflows and buying cloud services.
limits: firm self-report; early low adoption; rotating panel

title: Automation, AI, and the Intergenerational Transmission of Knowledge
finding: In an overlapping-generations model where novices learn tacit knowledge from experts, better entry-level automation raises output but can lower growth and welfare, even without cutting entry-level jobs, if it shifts novices away from the most productive experts.
limits: theoretical model; no data

title: The Flaws of Policies Requiring Human Oversight of Government Algorithms
finding: A review of 41 policies requiring human oversight of government algorithms concludes that people generally cannot perform the oversight functions these policies assume, so the policies can legitimise flawed algorithms and dilute accountability; proposes institutional oversight requiring evidence that any human oversight works.
limits: policy review; no new data

title: Human-AI interactions in public sector decision making: 'automation bias' and 'selective adherence' to algorithmic advice
venue: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory
finding: Three survey experiments found no automation bias (algorithmic advice was not followed more than equivalent human-expert advice), but citizens followed advice more when it matched ethnic stereotypes; civil servants did not.
limits: vignette task; hypothetical decision

title: 'Just like I thought': Street-level bureaucrats trust AI recommendations if they confirm their professional judgment
n: Dutch police officers (n not on page read)
finding: In a 2x2 experiment with a mock predictive-policing system, police officers trusted and followed AI recommendations mainly when these matched their own professional judgment, and explanations did not change trust.
limits: vignette; mock system

title: Putting a human in the loop: Increasing uptake, but decreasing accuracy of automated decision-making
finding: Letting people adjust an algorithm's output raised uptake by 7 percentage points but made decisions less accurate (error 18.0 vs 17.4), and people were less likely to intervene on large errors (60%) than small ones (64%).
limits: lab task; lay participants; verified in earlier pass only

title: Algorithmic risk assessment in the hands of humans
finding: Judges changed sentencing after a risk tool was introduced but departed from it in systematic ways, and the tool brought no detectable gain in public safety or fall in incarceration.
limits: single jurisdiction; working paper

title: If you give a judge a risk score: evidence from Kentucky bail decisions
venue: Harvard Olin Center Fellows' Discussion Paper
finding: When Kentucky made risk-score recommendations the default, judges followed lenient recommendations more often, but overrode them more for Black than for white defendants.
limits: single state; working paper

title: Algorithmic recommendations and human discretion
venue: NBER Working Paper 31747 (Review of Economic Studies 2026 per NBER page)
finding: About 90% of bail judges did worse than the algorithm when they overrode it, while the top 10% beat it on accuracy and fairness by using private information.
limits: one court system; outcomes only partly observed

title: Human Decisions and Machine Predictions
finding: Using quasi-random judge assignment in New York City bail cases, a machine-learning model could have cut crime by up to 24.7% with no change in jailing, or cut jailing by up to 41.9% with no rise in crime, implying judges misweigh observable risk.
limits: simulated policy; effect sizes from abstract not re-read (page truncated)

title: Discretion in hiring
finding: Hiring managers who overrode a job-test's recommendations more often made hires who stayed for shorter periods, suggesting that discretion lowered hire quality.
limits: pre-AI job testing; tenure as quality proxy

title: A Case for Humans-in-the-Loop: Decisions in the Presence of Erroneous Algorithmic Scores
n: child-maltreatment hotline screening decisions (n not on page read)
finding: When a software error displayed incorrect risk scores to child-welfare hotline screeners, they were less likely to follow the tool's recommendation for erroneous scores, even when overriding required supervisor approval.
limits: one agency; pre-generative tool

title: How Child Welfare Workers Reduce Racial Disparities in Algorithmic Decisions
finding: Screeners' decisions made with the Allegheny Family Screening Tool showed smaller Black-white disparities in screen-in rates than the tool's scores alone would have produced.
limits: one county; not rechecked

title: Appropriateness of Overridden Alerts in Computerized Physician Order Entry: Systematic Review
finding: Across 23 studies, clinicians overrode 46.2%-96.2% of computerised order-entry safety alerts on average, and the share of overrides judged appropriate ranged from 29.4% to 100% by alert type.
limits: heterogeneous studies; rule-based alerts

cite: van der Sijs, Aarts, Vulto & Berg 2006
title: Overriding of Drug Safety Alerts in Computerized Physician Order Entry
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association 13(2)
finding: A systematic review found drug safety alerts were overridden in 49%-96% of cases, with alert fatigue and low specificity as recurrent reasons.
limits: rule-based alerts; not rechecked

title: Liable, but Not in Control? Ensuring Meaningful Human Agency in Automated Decision-Making Systems
finding: Argues many automated systems keep a human only nominally in the loop ('quasi-automation'), leaving that person liable without real control, and proposes criteria for meaningful human agency over automated decisions.
limits: conceptual; not rechecked

title: Humans in the Loop
finding: Catalogues the distinct roles a human in the loop is expected to play (such as correcting errors, providing accountability and preserving dignity) and argues that adding a human does not by itself secure any of them.
limits: legal theory; not rechecked

title: Institutionalised Distrust and Human Oversight of Artificial Intelligence: Towards a Democratic Design of AI Governance under the European Union AI Act
finding: Argues human oversight under the EU AI Act is hard to make effective because overseers may lack competence and face distorted incentives, and proposes separating first-degree overseers (who shape decisions) from second-degree overseers (who review them), built on six democratic principles of institutionalised distrust.
limits: conceptual

title: On the Quest for Effectiveness in Human Oversight: Interdisciplinary Perspectives
finding: Proposes that a human overseer is effective only with sufficient causal power, suitable epistemic access, self-control and fitting intentions, maps technical, individual and environmental facilitators and inhibitors, and assesses EU AI Act Article 14 against this account.
limits: conceptual; no empirical test

cite: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme 2023
title: Report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
finding: The inquiry into Australia's 2016-2020 automated income-averaging debt scheme found it unlawful and unfair, with legal and oversight checks failing for years; about 470,000 debts were wrongly raised and a A$1.872bn class-action settlement followed.
limits: rule-based automation, not AI; figures via earlier pass

title: Xenophobic Machines: Discrimination through Unregulated Use of Algorithms in the Dutch Childcare Benefits Scandal
finding: Analysis of the Dutch childcare-benefits scandal (about 26,000 parents wrongly accused of fraud) found the tax authority's risk-classification model used nationality as a risk factor and that flagged cases faced harsh scrutiny with weak checks.
limits: advocacy report; not rechecked

title: A Tale of Two Algorithms: The Appeal and Repeal of Calculated Grades Systems in England and Ireland in 2020
finding: Compares England's and Ireland's 2020 statistical grade-calculation systems, both abandoned after public backlash in favour of teacher-assessed grades.
limits: two cases; not rechecked

title: Government by Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence in Federal Administrative Agencies
venue: Report to the Administrative Conference of the United States
n: canvass of 142 federal agencies; 7 case studies
finding: First systematic canvass of AI use across 142 US federal agencies, with seven case studies of how agencies acquire and oversee AI; a baseline for later federal inventories.
limits: pre-generative; snapshot

title: The Bureaucratic Challenge to AI Governance: An Empirical Assessment of Implementation at U.S. Federal Agencies
n: US federal agencies under three AI legal mandates (n unclear)
finding: Fewer than 40% of the legal requirements examined under US federal AI executive orders and statute could be verified as implemented, including gaps in agencies' AI use-case inventories.
limits: compliance audit; page could not be fetched

title: Artificial Intelligence: Agencies Have Begun Implementation but Need to Complete Key Requirements (GAO-24-105980)
finding: 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases (about 200 in use), but only 5 gave complete information for every use case and only 10 had fully implemented applicable AI requirements; GAO made 35 recommendations.
limits: compliance audit; no decision counts

title: Federal Agency AI Use Case Inventories (2023, 2024, 2025)
venue: US Office of Management and Budget (GitHub)
finding: Disclosed federal AI use cases rose from 710 (2023) to 2,133 (2024) and 3,611 (2025, 445 high-impact), but the inventories record no counts of decisions affected or of human overrides.
limits: disclosure counts; definitional breaks; figures via earlier pass

title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard records (compared with Public Law Project's TAG register)
finding: Official UK algorithmic transparency records grew from 6 (Oct 2023) to 152 (Oct 2026) after the standard became mandatory for central government, while an NGO register had already found 55 government tools in Oct 2023.
limits: counts tools, not decisions; mandate-driven growth; figures via earlier pass

title: Algoritmeregister (Dutch national Algorithm Register) dashboard
finding: Published algorithm descriptions by Dutch public bodies rose from 1,224 (Nov 2025) to 1,574 (Oct 2026), though only 354 of 530 connected organisations had published any entry.
limits: not mandatory for all; includes rule-based systems; figures via earlier pass

title: DSA Transparency Database (statements of reasons for content moderation)
n: 3,944,217,973 statements of reasons in a rolling 180-day window
finding: Online platforms reported about 3.94 billion moderation decisions in the latest 180 days, 43% flagged as fully automated, making it the largest public per-decision count of automated decisions found in this search.
limits: platform self-report; 'automated' is not always AI

title: Use of artificial intelligence in government
n: UK government bodies (n not on page read)
finding: A government-wide survey found AI not yet widely used, with 70% of respondents piloting or planning AI use cases, and named legacy systems and data access as basic barriers alongside the need for a realistic skills and workforce plan.
limits: self-report snapshot

title: SAFO 13002: Manual Flight Operations
finding: The regulator warned that continuous use of autoflight 'could lead to degradation of the pilot's ability' to recover from undesired states and urged operators to build manual flying into policy, training and checks.
limits: advisory, not a study

cite: US DOT Office of Inspector General 2016
title: Enhanced FAA Oversight Could Reduce Hazards Associated With Increased Use of Flight Deck Automation (AV-2016-013)
n: 9 air carriers; 19 initial simulator training plans
finding: Three years after SAFO 13002, the FAA could not tell how often pilots fly manually, only 5 of 19 training plans addressed pilot monitoring, 2 of 9 carriers discouraged manual flying, and the FAA had not ensured training developed manual skills.
limits: audit; no skill testing

title: Patriot Wars: Automation and the Patriot Air and Missile Defense System
venue: Center for a New American Security
finding: Analysis of the 2003 Patriot fratricides (2 of 11 ballistic-missile engagements) attributes them to near all-or-none automation, naive trust and under-trained crews, arguing automation raised training needs and that post-incident changes did not substantially lengthen training.
limits: single expert analysis; military

title: AI Hallucination Cases Database
n: 2,184 court and tribunal decisions (as of 10 Oct 2026)
finding: Courts and tribunals have issued 2,184 decisions addressing hallucinated AI content in filings (10 Oct 2026; 712 at end-Dec 2025 per an earlier pass), involving self-represented litigants in 1,259, lawyers in 864 and judges in 32, mostly in the US (1,492).
limits: only decisions that address AI; undercounts fake citations

cite: Magesh, Surani, Dahl, Suzgun, Manning & Ho 2024
title: Hallucination-free? Assessing the reliability of leading AI legal research tools
venue: arXiv (later Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, not checked)
finding: Commercial RAG legal research tools (Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, Ask Practical Law AI) hallucinated on 17-33% of queries, fewer than GPT-4 but far from 'hallucination-free'.
limits: no human-user component; 2024 products

title: The AI Review Lottery: Widespread AI-Assisted Peer Reviews Boost Paper Scores and Acceptance Rates
finding: At least 15.8% of ICLR 2024 reviews were AI-assisted (detector lower bound); AI-assisted reviews gave the higher score in 53.4% of discordant pairs, and near-threshold papers with one were 4.9 percentage points more likely to be accepted.
limits: detector-based; one conference

title: Mapping the Increasing Use of LLMs in Scientific Papers
finding: LLM-modified content in papers rose steadily after ChatGPT, reaching an estimated up to 17.5% in computer science and up to 6.3% in mathematics and Nature-portfolio papers, and was higher for frequent preprint posters, crowded fields and shorter papers.
limits: population estimate; measures writing, not reasoning

title: Artificial Intelligence in the News: How AI Retools, Rationalizes, and Reshapes Journalism and the Public Arena
venue: Tow Center for Digital Journalism, Columbia University
n: interviews with news workers and experts (n unclear)
finding: Interviews across news organisations indicate that relying on AI infrastructure and models from a few large technology firms deepens newsrooms' dependence on platform companies and shifts control over news-production tools.
limits: qualitative; report page blocked, not rechecked

title: Does automation bias decision-making?
finding: In a simulated flight-monitoring task, people using an automated aid made omission errors (missing events the aid did not flag) and commission errors (following wrong aid directives), the two classic forms of automation bias.
limits: simulated task; student sample; details not re-checked this session

title: Complacency and bias in human use of automation: an attentional integration
finding: Review arguing that automation complacency and automation bias share attentional roots, affect novices and experts alike, and are not reliably removed by training or instructions.
limits: narrative review; pre-AI automation

title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
finding: Systematic review finding automation bias in clinical decision support is common, with wrong advice raising commission errors, and with experience, confidence, trust, task complexity and workload as mediators.
limits: pre-LLM decision support; heterogeneous studies

title: Automation bias and verification complexity: a systematic review
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
finding: Review concluding that automation bias is more likely when checking the aid's output is complex or workload is high, because people use the aid in place of vigilant checking.
limits: pre-LLM; mixed domains

title: Algorithm aversion: people erroneously avoid algorithms after seeing them err
finding: After seeing a forecasting algorithm make errors, people were less likely to choose it over their own less accurate forecasts, which lowered their accuracy.
limits: forecasting tasks; online and lab samples

title: Algorithm appreciation: people prefer algorithmic to human judgment
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
finding: Lay participants gave more weight to advice labelled as coming from an algorithm than from people, while experienced national-security professionals discounted advice and lost accuracy.
limits: estimation tasks; label manipulation only

title: A systematic review of algorithm aversion in augmented decision making
finding: Review grouping causes of algorithm aversion into themes such as false expectations, lack of decision control and clashes with intuition, and proposing design responses.
limits: pre-LLM literature

title: Disparate interactions: an algorithm-in-the-loop analysis of fairness in risk assessments
finding: Online participants given a pretrial risk score did not beat the score alone, could not judge their own or the score's accuracy, and deviated from it in racially disparate ways.
limits: lay participants, not judges

title: Combining human expertise with artificial intelligence: experimental evidence from radiology
finding: AI predictions did not improve radiologists' accuracy on average, because they gave the AI too little weight and treated its signal as independent of their own.
limits: chest X-ray reading; experimental setting

cite: Yu, Moehring, Banerjee, Salz, Agarwal, Rajpurkar et al. 2024
title: Heterogeneity and predictors of the effects of AI assistance on radiologists
finding: AI assistance helped some radiologists and hurt others; experience, subspecialty and unassisted skill did not predict who benefited, and inaccurate AI predictions worsened performance.
limits: retrospective cases; one AI model

title: Automation Bias in Mammography: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence BI-RADS Suggestions on Reader Performance
finding: When the AI's BI-RADS suggestion was wrong, accuracy fell from ~80% to under 20% for inexperienced readers and from 82% to 45.5% for very experienced readers.
limits: non-generative AI; deliberately wrong AI; small reader panel; measures in-the-moment bias, not lasting skill; read via RSNA press release

cite: Jabbour, Fouhey, Shepard, ... Sjoding et al. 2023
title: Measuring the impact of AI in the diagnosis of hospitalized patients: a randomized clinical vignette survey study
finding: A standard AI model raised clinicians' diagnostic accuracy from 73% by 2.9 to 4.4 points, but a systematically biased model cut it by 11.3 points, and explanations did not prevent the drop.
limits: vignettes; simulated model

title: Do as AI say: susceptibility in deployment of clinical decision-aids
finding: Inaccurate advice lowered physicians' diagnostic accuracy whether it was labelled AI or human, and about 28% of radiologists and 42% of IM/EM physicians never caught the wrong advice.
limits: 8 cases; advice actually written by humans

title: Human-computer collaboration for skin cancer recognition
finding: Good AI support improved skin-lesion diagnosis, most for the least experienced, but faulty AI misled clinicians at every experience level, including experts.
limits: web reader platform; image-only task

cite: Jacobs, Pradier, McCoy, Perlis, Doshi-Velez & Gajos 2021
title: How machine-learning recommendations influence clinician treatment selections: the example of antidepressant selection
finding: Incorrect ML recommendations lowered clinicians' treatment-selection accuracy below their no-advice baseline (0.299 vs 0.357), explanations did not offset this, and confidence did not change.
limits: vignettes; simulated recommendations

title: Does the whole exceed its parts? The effect of AI explanations on complementary team performance
finding: Human-AI teams beat either alone on three tasks, but explanations did not add to that gain and instead made people accept AI recommendations more often, including wrong ones.
limits: crowd workers; lab tasks

title: To trust or to think: cognitive forcing functions can reduce overreliance on AI in AI-assisted decision-making
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
finding: Cognitive forcing designs (e.g. deciding before seeing AI advice) reduced over-reliance on wrong AI suggestions more than simple explanations, but were the least liked, and people high in need for cognition benefited most.
limits: nutrition task; online sample

title: Effect of confidence and explanation on accuracy and trust calibration in AI-assisted decision making
finding: Showing the AI's confidence score helped people calibrate trust, but calibrated trust alone did not improve joint accuracy, and local explanations did not help.
limits: income-prediction style task; online sample

cite: Vasconcelos, Jörke, Grunde-McLaughlin, Gerstenberg, Bernstein & Krishna 2023
title: Explanations can reduce overreliance on AI systems during decision-making
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
finding: Across five maze studies, explanations reduced over-reliance only when they made checking the AI cheaper than simply following it; task difficulty, explanation difficulty and pay all shifted reliance.
limits: maze task; simulated AI

title: Do people engage cognitively with AI? Impact of AI assistance on incidental learning
finding: AI recommendations, with or without explanations, improved nutrition decisions but produced no learning, while explanations without a recommendation improved both decisions and learning.
limits: nutrition task; single session; learning test details not re-checked

title: Knowing about knowing: an illusion of human competence can hinder appropriate reliance on AI systems
finding: People who overestimated their own ability (a Dunning-Kruger pattern) under-relied on AI advice; a tutorial exposing AI errors improved calibration for over-estimators but could harm under-estimators.
limits: logical-reasoning task; crowd sample

title: Appropriate reliance on AI advice: conceptualization and the effect of explanations
finding: Proposes 'Appropriateness of Reliance' as a two-part measure (relying on correct and rejecting incorrect advice) and shows in an experiment that explanations of AI advice shift it.
limits: single task; measure proposal

title: Understanding the role of human intuition on reliance in human-AI decision-making with explanations
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
finding: Feature-based explanations increased over-reliance on wrong AI predictions, whereas example-based explanations helped people apply their own intuition and reach complementary performance.
limits: think-aloud; two prediction tasks

title: Towards a science of human-AI decision making: a survey of empirical studies
finding: Maps 100+ human-subject studies of AI-assisted decisions by task, type of AI assistance and evaluation metric, and finds few shared frameworks across them.
limits: pre-LLM literature

title: Overreliance on AI: literature review
finding: Review of about 60 papers that defines over-reliance as accepting incorrect AI outputs and summarises its causes, measurement, consequences and mitigations.
limits: industry report; pre-LLM evidence

cite: Goh, Gallo, Hom, ... Chen et al. 2024
title: Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial
finding: GPT-4 access did not improve physicians' diagnostic reasoning scores (76% vs 74%), while GPT-4 alone scored 92%, 16 points above the control group.
limits: vignettes; small sample; little prompting training

title: GPT-4 assistance for improvement of physician performance on patient care tasks: a randomized controlled trial
finding: Physicians using GPT-4 scored 6.5 points higher on management reasoning (43.0% vs 35.7%) and took about 2 minutes longer per case; GPT-4 alone scored about the same as GPT-4-assisted physicians.
limits: vignettes; simulated setting

cite: McDuff, Schaekermann, Tu, ... Natarajan et al. 2025
title: Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
finding: Clinicians helped by the LLM reached 51.7% top-10 differential accuracy, versus 36.1% unassisted and 44.4% with search, while the LLM alone reached 59.1%.
limits: published case challenges; developer-run study

cite: Qazi, Ali, Khawaja, Akhtar, Sheikh & Alizai 2025
title: Automation bias in large language model assisted diagnostic reasoning among AI-trained physicians
finding: Physicians who had completed AI-literacy training and received deliberately wrong ChatGPT-4o suggestions in half their cases scored 14 points lower on diagnostic reasoning (73.3% vs 84.9%) than those given correct suggestions.
limits: preprint; small sample; vignettes

cite: Qazi, Ali, Khawaja, Akhtar, Sheikh & Alizai 2026
title: Mitigating automation bias in physician-LLM diagnostic reasoning using behavioral nudges: a randomized controlled trial
finding: Adding a benchmark-accuracy cue and a per-case traffic-light reliability rating to ChatGPT-5.1 suggestions (half deliberately wrong) raised physicians' diagnostic reasoning scores by 7.6 points.
limits: preprint; vignettes

cite: Bean, Payne, Parsons, Kirk, ... Rocher & Mahdi 2026
title: Reliability of LLMs as medical assistants for the general public: a randomized preregistered study
finding: LLMs alone identified relevant conditions in 94.9% of scenarios, but members of the public using them did so in under 34.5% and chose the right course of action in under 44.2%, no better than controls.
limits: hypothetical scenarios; 2024-era models

title: Fact-checking information from large language models can decrease headline discernment
finding: LLM fact-checks did not improve people's ability to tell true from false headlines on average, lowered belief in true headlines the AI mislabelled, and raised belief in false headlines when the AI was unsure.
limits: political headlines; one model

cite: Si, Goyal, Wu, Zhao, Feng, Daumé & Boyd-Graber 2024
title: Large language models help humans verify truthfulness - except when they are convincingly wrong
finding: LLM explanations made fact-checking faster with accuracy similar to search, but people over-relied on wrong explanations; contrastive explanations reduced this without beating search.
limits: small crowd sample

title: Effects of LLM-based search on decision making: speed, accuracy, and overreliance (earlier title: Comparing traditional and LLM-based search for consumer choice)
finding: LLM-based search sped up consumer decisions with accuracy similar to traditional search when the LLM was right, but people over-relied on it when it erred; confidence-based highlighting improved error detection.
limits: consumer product task; planted errors

title: The decision to verify: how warmth and user characteristics shape reliance on conversational agents for information search
finding: Even with web search available, people relied on a chatbot's answers; whether they checked depended mainly on prior trust in chatbots, and a warm conversational style increased agreement with wrong answers.
limits: preprint; QA task

cite: Kim, Wortman Vaughan, Liao, Lombrozo & Russakovsky 2025
title: Fostering appropriate reliance on large language models: the role of explanations, sources, and inconsistencies
finding: LLM explanations increased reliance on both correct and incorrect answers, while showing sources or inconsistencies within explanations reduced reliance on incorrect answers.
limits: objective QA questions; online sample

title: To rely or not to rely? Evaluating interventions for appropriate reliance on large language models
finding: Reliance interventions reduced over-reliance on wrong LLM advice on LSAT and estimation tasks but generally did not improve appropriate reliance, and people sometimes grew more confident after wrong reliance choices.
limits: preprint; two lab tasks

title: Trust and reliance on AI: an experimental study on the extent and costs of overreliance on AI
finding: In an incentivised experiment, people followed advice labelled as AI even when it contradicted context and their own assessment, producing worse outcomes for themselves and third parties.
limits: Prolific sample; abstract-level check only

title: People devalue generative AI's competence but not its advice in addressing societal and personal challenges
finding: People rated a disclosed AI author as less competent than a human expert but did not rate its advice lower or say they were less likely to follow it.
limits: stated intentions, not behaviour

title: No thoughts just AI: biased LLM hiring recommendations alter human decision making and limit human autonomy
finding: With race-biased simulated AI recommendations, people picked the AI's favoured group in up to 90% of resume-screening choices, versus equal rates without AI or with unbiased AI.
limits: simulated AI; lay screeners

title: AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: Access to a GPT-4 forecasting assistant improved accuracy by 24-28% against a weaker control model, even when the assistant was built to give overconfident, base-rate-neglecting advice.
limits: six questions; one outlier item

title: AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking
finding: Self-reported AI use correlated with cognitive offloading (r=+0.72) and lower critical thinking (r=-0.68), with offloading partly mediating the link.
limits: cross-sectional self-report; correction issued Sept 2025

cite: Fernandes, Villa, Nicholls, Haavisto, Buschek, Schmidt, Kosch, Shen & Welsch 2025
title: AI makes you smarter but none the wiser: the disconnect between performance and metacognition
finding: ChatGPT raised LSAT reasoning scores by about 3.5 of 20 points, but users overestimated their scores by about 4 points, the usual Dunning-Kruger pattern vanished, and higher AI literacy went with more overconfidence.
limits: online samples; most users sent one prompt per item

title: Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry
finding: Students who researched a science question with ChatGPT reported lower cognitive load than Google users but wrote lower-quality justifications, with no difference in diversity of recommendations.
limits: small sample; single task

title: Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on learning motivation, processes, and performance
finding: ChatGPT support gave the largest essay-score improvement among four arms (ChatGPT, human expert, writing analytics, none) but no difference in knowledge gain or transfer, with altered self-regulated learning sequences the authors call 'metacognitive laziness'.
limits: single writing task; 'metacognitive laziness' is an interpretation of process logs; AI-free status of knowledge test not confirmed

title: The effects of over-reliance on AI dialogue systems on students' cognitive abilities: a systematic review
finding: Review of 14 studies linking over-reliance on AI dialogue systems with weaker critical thinking, decision-making and analytical reasoning in students.
limits: small, mostly descriptive evidence base

cite: Tankelevitch, Kewenig, Simkute, Scott, Sarkar, Sellen & Rintel 2024
title: The metacognitive demands and opportunities of generative AI
finding: Argues that GenAI places high metacognitive demands on users (setting goals, judging outputs, deciding when to use AI) and proposes building metacognitive support into systems.
limits: conceptual; no new data

title: "AI enhances our performance, I have no doubt this one will do the same": the placebo effect is robust to negative descriptions of AI
finding: People told a sham AI would adapt their interface expected better results and performed descriptively better, even when told the AI would hinder them.
limits: sham AI; simple perceptual task

title: The Widening Gap: The Benefits and Harms of Generative AI for Novice Programmers
finding: Students already doing well used GenAI to accelerate, while struggling novices had their metacognitive difficulties compounded and left with an 'illusion of competence', overrating their own ability.
limits: small qualitative sample; single problem

title: Do users write more insecure code with AI assistants?
finding: Participants with a Codex-based assistant wrote significantly less secure code yet were more likely to believe it was secure; those who trusted the AI less produced fewer vulnerabilities.
limits: security tasks; 2022 model

title: Students' reliance on AI in higher education: identifying contributing factors
finding: Undergraduates who accepted deliberately wrong AI programming suggestions reported higher post-task trust and satisfaction, while appropriate reliance went with self-efficacy, programming literacy and need for cognition.
limits: preprint; correlational within experiment

title: Thinking - fast, slow, and artificial: how AI is reshaping human reasoning and the rise of cognitive surrender
finding: In preregistered reasoning experiments people often adopted deliberately wrong AI answers and grew more confident; incentives with feedback raised override rates and time pressure lowered them (figures unconfirmed against the paper).
limits: working paper; not read this session

title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
finding: GPT-4 raised task completion 12.2%, speed 25.1% and quality >40% inside the AI frontier, but consultants using it were 19 pp less likely to get a correct answer on a task just outside it.
limits: GPT-4 (2023); one firm; no unaided test after use

title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
finding: Developers expected AI to cut task time by 24% and afterwards believed it had cut it by 20%, but AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer; in METR's 2026 follow-up, 30-50% of developers avoided submitting tasks they did not want to do without AI.
limits: 16 experts on familiar repos; early-2025 tools; follow-up figures from prior pass, not re-checked

title: Contrastive explanations that anticipate human misconceptions can improve human decision-making skills
finding: Explanations contrasting the AI's choice with the person's predicted choice improved people's independent decision-making skill more than standard explanations, without lowering assisted accuracy.
limits: exercise-choice task; single session; predictive model with LLM-phrased explanations

title: Large legal fictions: profiling legal hallucinations in large language models
n: n/a (model evaluation on federal court cases)
finding: General LLMs hallucinated on 58% (GPT-4) to 88% (Llama 2) of verifiable case-specific legal questions, often accepted users' false legal premises, and could not reliably tell when they were hallucinating.
limits: 2023 models; no human users

title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
finding: In a crossover RCT, students learning from a scaffolded GPT-4 tutor scored higher on the post-lesson quiz than after in-class active learning (median 4.5 vs 3.5; ~0.73-1.3 SD by quantile regression) in less time (median 49 min).
limits: two lessons; immediate quiz only; whether AI was available during the quiz not stated on page; heavily scaffolded tutor

title: AI Meets the Classroom: When Do Large Language Models Harm Learning?
n: unclear (two pre-registered lab experiments plus a field study)
finding: No net effect of LLM access on learning; students who used LLMs to substitute (e.g. generate solutions) covered more topics but understood each less, those who used them to complement (e.g. ask for explanations) understood more, and LLMs widened the gap between low- and high-prior-knowledge students.
limits: whether the outcome test was AI-free not confirmed from abstract; sample sizes not on abstract page

title: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125
finding: Six weeks of teacher-guided after-school English tutoring with Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) raised a composite assessment by 0.31 SD and English by 0.23 SD, with larger gains for girls and higher-baseline students.
limits: 6 weeks; facilitated by teachers; assessment conditions (AI-free) not stated on page; no follow-up on retention

title: Effective and Scalable Math Support: Evidence on the Impact of an AI-Tutor on Math Achievement in Ghana
finding: Two 30-minute sessions a week with Rori (an LLM-based WhatsApp maths tutor) over 8 months raised maths growth scores by 0.37 relative to control schools.
limits: school-level assignment with few schools; test conditions not stated on abstract; no retention follow-up

title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
n: 900 tutors randomised (782 at launch), ~1,800 K-12 students
finding: Giving tutors real-time LLM guidance raised students' exit-ticket mastery by 4 pp (62% to 66%) and by 9 pp for students of lower-rated tutors, with tutors asking more guiding questions; no significant end-of-year test effect.
limits: about 2 months; tutors' own skill without the tool was not measured (listed as future work)

title: Experimental evidence of the effects of large language models versus web search on depth of learning
finding: People who learned a topic from LLM summaries rather than web links developed shallower knowledge and later wrote sparser, less original advice that others were less likely to adopt, even when the LLM output included links.
limits: single sessions; online samples; advice-writing is a proxy for depth of knowledge

title: The effect of ChatGPT on students' learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
finding: Reported a large effect of ChatGPT on learning performance (g = 0.867) and moderate effects on perception and higher-order thinking (~0.46), but was retracted in 2026 over discrepancies (inconsistent study counts, weighting, a retracted included study).
limits: RETRACTED; link is the retraction notice; many pooled studies let the AI group use ChatGPT during the post-test (Lawson et al. 2026)

title: Does ChatGPT enhance student learning? A systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies
finding: Pooled experimental studies show positive associations of ChatGPT use with academic performance, affective-motivational states and higher-order thinking, lower mental effort, and no change in self-efficacy.
limits: pooled effect sizes not confirmed this session; most included studies poorly controlled (Lawson et al. 2026; Weidlich et al. 2025)

title: Color Me Confounded: A Critical Analysis of Media Comparisons on ChatGPT in Education
n: 63 comparisons (Deng et al.) and 46 (Wang & Fan) double-coded
finding: Only 6 of 63 (Deng) and 3 of 46 (Wang & Fan) ChatGPT-vs-control comparisons controlled instructional method, practice and time, only 1-2 'direct learning' wins were comparable, and 7-8 comparisons let the ChatGPT group use the tool during the post-test.
limits: pre-proof; codes reporting quality, not new outcome data

title: ChatGPT in Education: An Effect in Search of a Cause
n: audit of a subset of studies in Deng et al. 2025
finding: Argues ChatGPT-learning experiments repeat the old media-comparison confound; in an audit, only a small minority of Deng et al.'s primary studies described the treatment, the control and valid learning outcomes, so 'observed gains cannot, at this time, be confidently attributed to ChatGPT'.
limits: conceptual critique; partial audit

title: The GPT Surprise: Offering Large Language Model Chat in a Massive Coding Class Reduced Engagement but Increased Adopters' Exam Performances
finding: Offering GPT-4 chat in a free online coding course reduced exam participation and other engagement on average (but raised participation for students from low-HDI countries), while students who chose to use it scored higher on the exam.
limits: adopter gains are self-selected; exam AI policy not confirmed; one course

title: Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort (earlier title: Learning not cheating)
n: unclear (three pre-registered experiments plus a national survey of young adults)
finding: People who practised cover-letter writing with an AI tool exerted less effort yet wrote better letters in later no-AI tests than those practising alone, using Google, or getting human-editor feedback; merely viewing an AI-revised example gave similar gains.
limits: short-term; one genre (cover letters); sample sizes not on abstract page

title: Math Education with Large Language Models: Peril or Promise?
finding: LLM-generated explanations during practice improved later unaided maths performance more than seeing answers only, especially when people attempted problems first; even explanations with errors gave partial gains.
limits: single session; online adults; sample sizes not on page

title: Generative AI Usage and Exam Performance
finding: Students whose essays were flagged by AI detectors as GenAI-assisted scored on average 6.71 points lower (out of 100) on the later exam, with larger gaps among students with high learning potential.
limits: observational; GenAI use inferred from detectors; selection into use

title: Studying the effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners in Introductory Programming
finding: Codex access raised completion (1.15x) and scores (1.8x) during training, did not hurt AI-free code-modification tasks, and gave slightly (non-significantly) better scores on retention post-tests a week later, with benefits concentrated among learners with higher prior knowledge.
limits: Codex era (2022); young learners; small n

title: CodeAid: Evaluating a Classroom Deployment of an LLM-based Programming Assistant that Balances Student and Educator Needs
n: 700 students; 8,000 usages; 22 student and 8 educator interviews
finding: A semester-long deployment of an assistant designed to withhold full code solutions yielded design principles (promote cognitive engagement, avoid direct answers, keep students in control) but did not measure learning outcomes.
limits: no control group; no skill outcome

title: Predictive AI Can Support Human Learning while Preserving Error Diversity
n: unclear (medical novices; two pre-registered field experiments)
finding: AI input during training or practice each improved novices' later independent lung-cancer diagnoses, with both phases best, and AI changed how errors were distributed across people, which affected the accuracy of group second opinions.
limits: novices only; sample size and country not on abstract page

title: Diagnostic reasoning with and without AI: automation bias in pre-clerkship medical students
finding: Chatbot access raised diagnostic accuracy on average (largest gains for weaker students), but 26 students got worse, and students rated AI equally influential whether it helped or harmed them.
limits: single-group pre/post pilot; one case

title: Mixed-method review of AI-induced deskilling in medicine
finding: Finds 'conclusive evidence remains limited' for AI-induced clinical deskilling, that most sources are conceptual or interview-based, that 'upskilling inhibition' in trainees is under-studied and conflated with deskilling, and that no defined metrics exist.
limits: author names not confirmed on page read

cite: ESMO Real World Data & Digital Oncology 2026 scoping review (authors not confirmed)
title: Scoping review of automation bias and deskilling in clinical AI
venue: ESMO Real World Data and Digital Oncology
finding: Identifies only six primary investigations and describes evidence of clinical deskilling as scarce, with most quantitative findings about automation bias (e.g. 7% of correct pathology diagnoses reversed under AI influence).
limits: details from prior pass; not re-read this session

title: Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence
finding: ChatGPT cut writing-task time by 37% and raised graded quality by 0.45 SD, compressing differences between workers (task-to-task grade correlation 0.49 control vs 0.25 treated); two weeks later 33% of treated vs 18% of controls used ChatGPT at work.
limits: 20-30 minute tasks; no post-use unaided test; follow-up is usage only

title: AI Assistance in Legal Analysis: An Empirical Study
finding: GPT-4 assistance improved law students' scores on simple multiple-choice questions but not complex essays, helping bottom-of-class students greatly while top students' performance declined.
limits: sample size and randomisation details not on abstract page; GPT-4 (2023)

title: The Uneven Impact of Generative AI on Entrepreneurial Performance
finding: A GPT-4 business mentor via WhatsApp had no average effect, but high-baseline entrepreneurs gained just over 15% while low performers did about 8% worse, because of how they selected and implemented advice.
limits: sample size and duration not on page; business outcomes, not skill

title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI (earlier: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects)
n: unclear (Danish survey linked to admin records)
finding: Two years after ChatGPT, no detectable effect on earnings or hours (effects above 2% ruled out), though employers reorganised tasks and created new AI-oversight and integration work.
limits: labour outcomes only; no skill measure

title: Training with AI: Evidence from chess computers
n: unclear (chess players over staggered diffusion of chess computers)
finding: Players who gained access to chess computers improved their (unaided) tournament play, but did not learn to exploit idiosyncratic human mistakes, so the AI was an imperfect substitute for human training partners.
limits: non-LLM AI (chess engines, pre-2022 data); sample details not on page

title: Google effects on memory: Cognitive consequences of having information at our fingertips
finding: People primed to think of computers by hard questions and who expected information to stay accessible recalled it less well but remembered where it was stored.
limits: key 'Google Stroop' effect failed to replicate (Camerer et al. 2018; Hesselmann 2020); not re-read this session

title: No conclusive evidence that difficult general knowledge questions cause a 'Google Stroop effect'. A replication study
finding: A preregistered replication found no Google Stroop effect (BF01 = 5.07), echoing Camerer et al.'s (2018, Nature Human Behaviour) failed replication of Sparrow et al. 2011.
limits: tests only the priming component of Sparrow et al., not the memory-for-saved-information effect

title: Cognitive Offloading
finding: Defines cognitive offloading as using physical action or external tools to reduce cognitive demand and argues offloading decisions are driven by metacognitive evaluations of one's own abilities, which can be miscalibrated.
limits: conceptual review; not re-read this session

title: Using the Internet to access information inflates future use of the Internet to access other information
finding: People who had used the internet to answer earlier hard questions were more likely, and quicker, to turn to it for later easy questions they could have answered from memory.
limits: lab setting; details from memory, not re-read this session

title: Searching for explanations: How the Internet inflates estimates of internal knowledge
finding: Searching the internet for explanations led people to rate their own unaided knowledge higher, even in unrelated domains, confusing accessible knowledge with what they know.
limits: online samples; not re-read this session

title: Consequences of cognitive offloading: Boosting performance but diminishing memory
finding: More offloading made a copying task faster but reduced later memory for the material, an effect largely removed when people knew a memory test was coming.
limits: lab task; immediate memory test

title: Point-and-Shoot Memories: The Influence of Taking Photos on Memory for a Museum Tour
finding: Photographing whole museum objects impaired later memory for them (the 'photo-taking-impairment effect'), while zooming in on a detail removed the impairment.
limits: small field-lab studies; sample sizes not on page

title: Wayfinding with a GPS-based mobile navigation system: A comparison with maps and direct experience
finding: Pedestrians navigating with GPS travelled further, stopped more and formed poorer survey knowledge of the route than those using paper maps or direct experience.
limits: small field sample; details from memory, not re-read this session

title: GPS use negatively affects environmental learning through spatial transformation abilities
finding: Greater habitual GPS use was associated with poorer environmental learning, via weaker mental rotation and perspective-taking abilities.
limits: cross-sectional; details from memory, not re-read this session

title: Effects of hand-held calculators in precollege mathematics education: A meta-analysis
venue: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education
finding: Using calculators alongside traditional instruction generally did not harm, and often improved, students' paper-and-pencil skills and attitudes.
limits: pre-1986 studies; not re-read this session

title: The relationship between manual handling performance and recent flying experience in air transport pilots
finding: Pilots' manual handling performance in a simulated engine-failure task was associated with their amount of recent manual flying experience.
limits: cross-sectional; not re-read this session (page did not load)

title: Ironies of Automation
finding: Argues that automating routine work leaves humans to monitor and take over in rare abnormal situations, precisely when their unpractised manual and cognitive skills have decayed.
limits: conceptual; process-control setting; not re-read this session

title: The Out-of-the-Loop Performance Problem and Level of Control in Automation
finding: When an automated navigation expert system failed, operators who had been passive had lower situation awareness and slower decisions, and the level of control kept by the human moderated this out-of-the-loop effect.
limits: lab task; sample size not on page

title: Ironies of Generative AI: Understanding and mitigating productivity loss in human-AI interactions
finding: Maps Bainbridge-style ironies onto GenAI: users shift from producing to evaluating output, workflows are disrupted and interrupted, and easy tasks get easier while hard ones get harder.
limits: conceptual; journal venue not confirmed on page

title: Does using artificial intelligence assistance accelerate skill decay and hinder skill development without performers' awareness?
finding: Reviews skill-decay and learning research to argue that AI assistance may speed decay in experts and impede skill acquisition in learners while performers remain unaware of it.

title: LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning
finding: Frames tutoring as 'pedagogical instruction following'; expert raters preferred LearnLM over GPT-4o (+31%), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (+11%) and Gemini 1.5 Pro (+13%).
limits: developer-run evaluation; preference ratings, not student learning outcomes
